    3. The Fundamentals

    This chapter follows, script by script, the progression of chapter [The Fundamentals] from the TypeScript course: same sections, same order, with a Dart script corresponding to each TypeScript script.

    3.1. The Basics of Dart

    This first section covers the fundamentals common to all Dart programs: variables, lists, loops, functions, variable scope, basic types, and conversions.

    // basics_01.dart
// Ports the TypeScript script basics-01.ts: variables, arrays, loops,
// destructuring, functions, dynamic typing, comparison operators.
void main() {
  // constant - in Dart as in TypeScript, [const] declares a constant
  // whose value is known at COMPILE TIME (an even stricter constant
  // than TypeScript's [const], which only requires a value
  // known at run time and not reassigned)
  const String name = "dupont";
  // a screen display - [print] is the Dart equivalent of [console.log]
  print("name : $name");

  // an array (called a "list" in Dart) with elements of different types
  // [dynamic] because this list deliberately mixes several types
  // (demonstration) - it is the equivalent of TypeScript's [any]: Dart
  // then no longer performs any compile-time type checking
  // on the elements of this list
  final List<dynamic> array = ["one", "two", 3, 4];
  // its number of elements
  int n = array.length;
  // a loop
  for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    print("array[$i] = ${array[i]}");
  }

  // initialization of 2 variables with the content of a list
  // Dart has no list destructuring on assignment like
  // TypeScript (const [a, b] = array); since Dart 3, a
  // "list pattern" gives the same result (see dart3/*.dart
  // for a complete presentation of patterns)
  final [string1, string2] = ["string1", "string2"];
  // concatenation of the 2 strings
  final String string3 = string1 + string2;
  // display result
  print([string1, string2, string3]);
  // using a function
  display(string1);
  // the type of a variable can be known with runtimeType
  // (the Dart equivalent of TypeScript's [typeof] operator)
  displayType("n", n);
  displayType("string1", string1);
  displayType("array", array);

  // [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript] in TypeScript, the
  // [any] type allows a variable to change type during execution
  // (n = "has changed" after n = 4 is valid). In Dart, the type of a
  // variable is fixed once and for all by its declaration: [n] was
  // declared [int] above, so n = "has changed" is a COMPILATION
  // ERROR, not a mere oversight tolerated at run time. To
  // get a behaviour comparable to [any], one would have to declare
  // [dynamic n = array.length;] from the start - but this script
  // deliberately does not, in order to highlight the difference.
  // The following line is therefore COMMENTED OUT: uncommenting it causes a
  // compilation error.
  // n = "has changed";
  print('type[variable n]=${n.runtimeType} (Dart forbids assigning it '
      'anything other than an int: see the comment above)');

  // a function can return a result
  int res1 = f1(4);
  print("res1=$res1");

  // a function can return several values: Dart cannot return
  // a heterogeneous JS array directly into separate variables with
  // a syntax [let x, y, z; [x, y, z] = f()] like TypeScript. We use
  // either a Record (see dart3/, the modern typed solution), or here,
  // to stay close to the original script, a value that we destructure
  // with a pattern (Dart 3):
  final (res2, res3, res4) = f2();
  print("(res2,res3,res4)=${[res2, res3, res4]}");

  // we could have retrieved these values in a list
  final List<dynamic> t = f2ListAny();
  for (var i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
    print("t[$i]=${t[i]}");
  }
  // some tests
  for (var i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
    // displays only the strings - [is String] is the Dart equivalent of
    // [typeof(x) === "string"]
    if (t[i] is String) {
      print("t[$i]=${t[i]}");
    }
  }

  // [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Dart's
  // [==] operator ALWAYS corresponds to JavaScript's strict [===]
  // operator: Dart has no comparison operator with
  // implicit type conversion like JavaScript's non-strict [==].
  // The comparison "2" == 2 is therefore always false in Dart, whatever
  // the operator used - the code below therefore deliberately has
  // only one branch (no "with ==" then "with ===" section as
  // in the original TypeScript script, since this distinction does not exist).
  if ("2" == 2) {
    print("the string 2 is equal to the integer 2");
  } else {
    print("in Dart, the string '2' is never equal to the integer 2 "
        "(no implicit conversion like JS's non-strict ==)");
  }

  // other tests
  for (var i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
    // displays only the integers >10
    if (t[i] is int && t[i] > 10) {
      print("t[$i]=${t[i]}");
    }
  }

  // a while loop
  List<num> t2 = [8, 5, 0, -2, 3, 4];
  var i = 0;
  num sum = 0;
  while (i < t2.length && t2[i] > 0) {
    print("t2[$i]=${t2[i]}");
    sum += t2[i];
    i++;
  }
  print("sum=$sum");
}

// the main program stops here because there is no more executable code

// display
// ----------------------------------
void display(String string) {
  // displays string
  print("string=$string");
}

// displayType
// ----------------------------------
void displayType(String name, dynamic variable) {
  // displays the type of variable - [runtimeType] is the Dart equivalent of
  // [typeof]: unlike [typeof], which returns a generic string
  // ("number", "string"...), [runtimeType] returns the name of the REAL Dart
  // type of the value (int, String, List<dynamic>...)
  print("type[variable $name]=${variable.runtimeType}");
}

// ----------------------------------
int f1(int param) {
  // adds 10 to param
  return param + 10;
}

// ----------------------------------
// returns 3 values as a Record (Dart 3) - the modern, typed Dart type
// for what TypeScript would do with a heterogeneous array [any[]]
(String, int, int) f2() {
  return ("one", 0, 100);
}

// same result as f2(), but as a [dynamic] list to stay
// as close as possible to the [any[]] style of the original TypeScript script
List<dynamic> f2ListAny() {
  return ["one", 0, 100];
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 9: [const String name]: In Dart, [const] requires a value known at the time of COMPILATION — a stricter constraint than [const] for TypeScript, which only requires a value that has not been reassigned at runtime.
    • Line 18: [List<dynamic> array]: Dart calls the JavaScript “array” a [list], and [dynamic] plays the role of [any] in TypeScript to disable type checking on the elements.
    • Line 31: [final [string1, string2] = [...]]: Dart does not support destructuring assignments like TypeScript; the Dart 3 version LIST PATTERN, used here, yields the same result (a complete overview of the patterns is provided in the chapter [Dart 3.x New Features]).
    • Line 56: [n.runtimeType] replaces the [typeof] operator from TypeScript, with one difference: it returns a REAL Dart type name ([int], [List<dynamic>]...), not just a generic string (["number"], ["string"]).
    • The line [n = "has changed";] is intentionally commented out: unlike a variable [any] of type TypeScript, a Dart variable retains the type specified at its declaration—this assignment would result in a COMPILATION ERROR.
    • line 69: [final (res2, res3, res4) = f2();]: a Dart function cannot “return multiple values” into separate variables as a heterogeneous array TypeScript would; [f2] returns a RECORD (Dart 3) here, which is immediately destructured by a list pattern.
    • line 94: [if ("2" == 2)]: Dart’s [] operator corresponds to the strict [=] of JavaScript - There is no Dart equivalent for the non-strict [==] of JavaScript, so there is no second case to show here, unlike in the original TypeScript script.

    As a reminder, to run a Dart script, you can type the following command in a terminal:

    dart run path_to_script.dart

    For example, as shown below:

    dart run basics_01.dart

    if your terminal is set to the folder containing the script [basics_01.dart]. You can also click on the term [Run] in the text editor, which appears above the function [main]:

    // basics_02.dart
// Ports basics-02.ts: var/let/const in TypeScript, var/final/const in Dart.
void main() {
  // to initialize a variable, we use [var] (inferred type) or an
  // explicit type (like [int] here) for MUTABLE variables -
  // the equivalent of TypeScript's [let]
  int x = 4;
  x++;
  print(x);
  // [final] for a variable assigned ONLY ONCE at run time -
  // the equivalent of TypeScript's [const] (a value known only at
  // run time, but not reassignable afterwards)
  final int y = 10;
  x += y;
  // forbidden - x is mutable but y is not: y++ causes a
  // compilation error, exactly as in TypeScript
  // y++;

  // [NEW compared to TypeScript] Dart offers a second keyword,
  // [const], stricter than [final]: a [const] constant must be
  // known at COMPILE TIME (as at the very beginning of basics_01.dart). There
  // is no equivalent of this final/const distinction in
  // TypeScript, where [const] only means "not reassigned".
  const int z = 100; // known at compile time: valid
  print(z);
}

    Let’s break down this code:

    • A mutable variable is declared with an explicit type (or [var]): this is equivalent to [let] from TypeScript.
    • [final] is the equivalent of [const] in TypeScript: a value assigned only once, but whose value is not known until runtime.
    • Line 19: [NEW] Dart adds a second keyword, [const], which is stricter than [final]: a value [const] must be known at the time of COMPILATION. TypeScript does not have this two-level distinction.

    The result of the execution is as follows:

    // basics_03.dart
// Ports basics-03.ts: variable scope - a file-level variable
// ("top-level" scope, the Dart equivalent of TypeScript's module
// scope) is visible from the functions of the same file.

// top-level variable (outside any function/class), like the top-level
// [let] of the TypeScript script
int count = 1;

void doSomething() {
  // count is known here: a function sees the top-level variables of
  // the file containing it, exactly as in TypeScript
  print("count=$count");
}

void main() {
  // call
  doSomething();
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • A variable declared outside any function (scope [top-level]) is visible from all functions in the same file—exactly the role of a module-scope variable in TypeScript.

    The result of execution is as follows:

    count=1

    // basics_04.dart
// Ports basics-04.ts: a variable local to a function hides a top-level
// variable with the same name - the same shadowing principle as in
// TypeScript.

// top-level variable
const int count = 1;

void doSomething() {
  // the local variable hides the top-level variable
  const count = 2;
  print("count inside function=$count");
}

void main() {
  // top-level variable
  print("count outside function=$count");
  // local variable
  doSomething();
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • A local variable within a function, with the same name as a top-level variable—HIDES it ([shadowing])—inside this function—the same principle as in TypeScript.

    // basics_05.dart
// Ports basics-05.ts: a variable declared inside a function
// is not known outside it - same principle as in TypeScript.
void doSomething() {
  // variable local to the function
  const count = 2;
  print("count inside function=$count");
}

void main() {
  // count is not known here: the following line, if uncommented,
  // would cause a compilation error ("Undefined name 'count'"),
  // exactly as in TypeScript
  // print("count outside function=$count");
  doSomething();
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • A variable declared inside a function is not visible outside of it: referencing it outside the function results in a compilation error, just as in TypeScript.

    The result of execution is as follows:

    count inside function=2

    // basics_06.dart
// Ports basics-06.ts: block scope.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] TypeScript has
// THREE declaration keywords with different scopes: [let] and [const]
// are BLOCK-scoped, but [var] (inherited from JavaScript) is
// FUNCTION-scoped - a [var] variable declared in a {...} block "leaks"
// outside that block, which is precisely what this script shows with [count3].
// Dart has NO equivalent of this [var]: [var], [final] and [const] are
// ALWAYS block-scoped in Dart, without exception. This script is therefore
// shorter than the original: there are only two cases to show, not three,
// and both behave like TypeScript's [let]/[const] cases.
void main() {
  // [var] (inferred type) defines a block-scoped variable
  {
    // the variable [count] is only known in this block
    var count = 1;
    print("count=$count");
  }
  // the variable [count] is not known here: the following line, if
  // uncommented, would cause a compilation error
  // count++;

  // [final] defines a (non-reassignable) block-scoped variable
  {
    // the variable [count2] is only known in this block
    final count2 = 1;
    print("count=$count2");
  }
  // the variable [count2] is not known here either
  // count2++;

  // there is no 3rd case in Dart: no declaration keyword
  // lets a variable "leak" outside the block where it is declared,
  // unlike the TypeScript/JavaScript [var] used for [count3]
  // in the original script.
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • [var] and [final] are ALWAYS BLOCK-scoped in Dart, without any exceptions.
    • This script shows only the TWO cases, whereas the TypeScript script showed three: Dart has no equivalent to [var] from JavaScript, whose scope is that of FUNCTION (not the block) and which “leaks” out of a [{...}] block—a classic source of bugs in JavaScript, but structurally impossible in Dart.

    // basics_07.dart
// Ports basics-07.ts: the main basic data types and their
// introspection with runtimeType (the Dart equivalent of typeof).
void main() {
  const int var1 = 10;
  const String var2 = "abc";
  const bool var3 = true;
  const List<int> var4 = [1, 2, 3];
  const Map<String, String> var5 = {'name': 'axèle'};
  // a variable of function type - Dart types functions with the
  // notation [ReturnType Function(parameters)]
  int Function() var6 = () => 3;

  // displaying the types with runtimeType
  print("var1.runtimeType=${var1.runtimeType}");
  print("var2.runtimeType=${var2.runtimeType}");
  print("var3.runtimeType=${var3.runtimeType}");
  print("var4.runtimeType=${var4.runtimeType}");
  print("var5.runtimeType=${var5.runtimeType}");
  print("var6.runtimeType=${var6.runtimeType}");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 12: [int Function() var6 = () => 3;]: In Dart, functions are defined using the notation [ReturnType Function(parameters)]—a function is a type like any other, assignable to a variable.
    • lines 15–20: [runtimeType] displays, for each variable, its real Dart type ([int], [String], [List<int>], [Map<String, String>] (line 9), [() => int]...).

// Ports basics-08.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] this script
// completely changes nature compared to the original. JavaScript (and
// therefore TypeScript, which only adds types checked at
// COMPILE TIME but keeps JavaScript's behaviour at RUN TIME)
// performs many IMPLICIT type conversions at run time:
// - in a test [if (data) ...], any value is converted to a
//   boolean ("" and 0 are "falsy", "abcd" and [1,2,3] are "truthy"...);
// - the [+] operator performs an addition IF BOTH operands are
//   numbers, otherwise a string concatenation ("12" * 1 is 12, but
//   "12" + 1 is "121");
// - true/false convert to 1/0 in a calculation...
// Dart has NONE of these implicit conversions:
// - the condition of an [if] must be a [bool], period: [if
//   ("abcd")] is a COMPILATION ERROR, not an automatic conversion;
// - [+] requires operands of the SAME type (String+String, or num+num): "12"
//   + 1 is a compilation error;
// - a [bool] is never implicitly converted to a number.
// This script therefore shows, unlike the original TypeScript script, the
// EXPLICIT conversions that must be written instead of each of these
// implicit conversions.
void main() {
  print("---------------[No implicit conversion to a boolean]------"
      "------------------------------");
  // in TypeScript, [showBool(value)] directly tests the "truthiness" of
  // any value. In Dart, you must write yourself the explicit
  // test matching what you really want to check: an empty
  // string, an empty list, a null value... [showBool] below
  // therefore deliberately accepts only an [Object?] (nullable) and documents,
  // for each family of types, the equivalent EXPLICIT conversion
  showBoolEquivalent("abcd", (v) => (v as String).isNotEmpty);
  showBoolEquivalent("", (v) => (v as String).isNotEmpty);
  showBoolEquivalent([1, 2, 3], (v) => (v as List).isNotEmpty);
  showBoolEquivalent(<int>[], (v) => (v as List).isNotEmpty);
  showBoolEquivalent(null, (v) => v != null);
  showBoolEquivalent(0.0, (v) => (v as double) != 0.0);
  showBoolEquivalent(0, (v) => (v as int) != 0);
  showBoolEquivalent(4.6, (v) => (v as double) != 0.0);

  print("---------------[Explicit conversion of a string to a number]"
      "------------------------------");
  showNumber("12");
  showNumber("45.67");
  showNumber("abcd");

  print("---------------[Explicit conversion to a boolean]------------"
      "------------------------------");
  // unlike Boolean(data) in JavaScript (which applies the
  // "truthiness" rules), there is no equivalent generic Dart function:
  // each type must provide its own notion of "empty/non-empty" (shown
  // above with showBoolEquivalent)

  print("---------------[Explicit conversion to a number]-------------"
      "-----------------------------");
  showNumber2("12.45");
  showNumber2(true); // this case is handled separately below
  showNumber2(null);

  print("---------------[Explicit conversion to a string]-------------"
      "-----------------------------");
  showString(5);
  showString(6.7);
  showString(false);
  showString(null);

  print("---------------[Other cases]------------------------------");
  const String string1 = '1000.78';
  // in Dart, [+] between a String and a num is a compilation error:
  // one of the two operands must be converted explicitly
  // conversion of string1 to a number, then addition
  final double data1 = double.parse(string1) + 1.034;
  print("data1=$data1 (explicit conversion required, unlike "
      "'1000.78' + 1.034 in JS which concatenates into a string)");
  // reverse conversion: the number to a string, then concatenation
  final String data2 = (1.034).toString() + string1;
  print("data2=$data2 (here we knowingly choose concatenation, by "
      "converting the number)");
  // true/false are NEVER implicitly converted to a number in Dart -
  // you must write the desired mapping yourself. [boolValue] is a
  // variable (and not the literal [true] directly): with a literal,
  // dart analyze would see the [: 0.0] branch as dead code (always
  // false), since the condition would then be known at compile time.
  // (deliberately [final], not [const]: a [const] would remain a compile-time
  // constant, and dart analyze would still detect the dead code)
  final bool boolValue = true;
  final double data3 = boolValue ? 1.0 : 0.0;
  print("data3=$data3 (explicit equivalent of JS's 'true * 1.18', "
      "combined with the multiplication below)");
  print("true converted then multiplied by 1.18 = ${data3 * 1.18}");
}

// displays, for a given value, the EXPLICIT boolean conversion that
// replaces JavaScript's implicit conversion - [tester] encodes the
// "right" way to test this particular value
void showBoolEquivalent(Object? data, bool Function(Object?) tester) {
  print("[data=$data], [type(data)]=${data.runtimeType}, "
      "[equivalent explicit test]=${tester(data)}");
}

void showNumber(String data) {
  // unlike [data * 1] in JS (which silently fails with NaN if
  // data is not numeric), [double.parse] throws an explicit
  // [FormatException] on failure - we catch it here to illustrate the
  // "abcd" case of the original script
  try {
    final number = double.parse(data);
    print("[data=$data], [number]=$number, [type(number)]="
        "${number.runtimeType}");
  } on FormatException {
    print("[data=$data] : FormatException, this is not a valid number "
        "(unlike Number('$data') in JS, which would return NaN without "
        "throwing an error)");
  }
}

void showNumber2(Object? data) {
  // explicit conversion according to the actual type of the data - there is no
  // single Dart function equivalent to Number(...) that would accept
  // a num, a bool or null indifferently
  double? number;
  if (data is num) {
    number = data.toDouble();
  } else if (data is String) {
    number = double.tryParse(data);
  } else if (data is bool) {
    number = data ? 1.0 : 0.0;
  }
  print("[data=$data], [type(data)]=${data.runtimeType}, [number]=$number, "
      "[type(number)]=${number.runtimeType}");
}

void showString(Object? data) {
  // toString() exists on (almost) every Dart object, including null
  // (returns "null") - quite close, here, to the behaviour of String(data)
  final String string = data.toString();
  print("[data=$data], [type(data)]=${data.runtimeType}, [string]=$string, "
      "[type(string)]=${string.runtimeType}");
}

    Let's discuss this code:

    • [showBoolEquivalent]: Dart does not have an implicit conversion to [bool]—a condition of type [if] requires a REAL [bool]; Each type family (string, list, number) must explicitly provide its own “empty/non-empty” test.
    • Line 126: [double.parse]/[double.tryParse] replace the implicit conversion [Number(string)] from JavaScript: [parse] raises an explicit [FormatException] on failure; [tryParse] returns [null]—never a silent [NaN].
    • Line 73: [double.parse(string1) + 1.034]: [+] between a [String] and a [num] is a COMPILATION error in Dart - unlike ['1000.78' + 1.034] to JavaScript, which concatenates silently.
    • [true ? 1.0 : 0.0]: [bool] is not implicitly converted to a number in Dart—you must write the desired mapping yourself, whereas [true * 1.18] is valid in JavaScript.

    // basics_09.dart
// Ports basics-09.ts (the modern ECMAScript 2020-2021 operators).
// Unlike the "ECMAScript new features", which will be replaced further on
// by the Dart 3.x New features chapter, this script stays HERE: most of
// these operators have existed natively in Dart for a long time (sometimes
// since Dart 2.0/2.12, well before 2020), so they are part of the
// Dart fundamentals just like the rest of this chapter.
void main() {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 1) the null-coalescing operator [??] - has existed in Dart for
  //    a long time (Dart 2.0), and behaves EXACTLY as in TypeScript:
  //    it only triggers the default value if the value is null (Dart
  //    has no [undefined] value separate from [null])
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // typed [int?] (nullable), not [int]: with a non-nullable type,
  // dart analyze would rightly see that [?? 10] can never
  // trigger (the type already guarantees that quantity1 is not null) - whereas
  // the goal here is precisely to compare the behaviour of [??] on
  // a non-null value (quantity1) and on a null value (quantity2)
  const int? quantity1 = 0;
  // in Dart, there is no [||] operator for this use: Dart's logical
  // [||] only accepts [bool] operands, so "quantity1 ||
  // 10" would be a compilation error - there is therefore only one
  // operator to show here, [??], without the risk of bug illustrated by the
  // original TypeScript script (0 is an [int] anyway, never
  // interpreted as "false")
  print("quantity1 ?? 10 = ${quantity1 ?? 10}"); // -> 0 (quantity1 is not null)

  const int? quantity2 = null;
  print("quantity2 ?? 10 = ${quantity2 ?? 10}"); // -> 10 (quantity2 is null)

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) optional chaining [?.] - has also existed in Dart for a long time
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  final person1 = PersonWithOptionalAddress(
    name: "Dupont",
    address: Address(city: "Nantes"),
  );
  final person2 = PersonWithOptionalAddress(name: "Martin"); // no address!

  // [?.] stops evaluation and returns [null] as soon as a step is null,
  // instead of throwing a "NoSuchMethodError" exception on null
  print("person1 city = ${person1.address?.city}");
  print("person2 city = ${person2.address?.city}"); // -> null, no error

  // [?.] and [??] can be combined to provide a fallback value
  print("person2 city (with default) = ${person2.address?.city ?? "unknown city"}");

  // [?.] also works on method calls...
  final objectWithMethod = ObjectWithMethod();
  print("existing method call : ${objectWithMethod.sayHello()}");
  // ...and on access to a list element (via the [?[ ]] operator)
  final List<int>? listOrNull = null;
  print("element of a missing list : ${listOrNull?[0]}"); // -> null

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) the logical assignment operators [??=]
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [a ??= b] is equivalent to [a = a ?? b]: assigns b only if a is null -
  // this one exists in Dart, with exactly the same syntax as in
  // TypeScript
  final config = Configuration(delay: 0, page: null);
  config.delay ??= 1000; // delay is already 0 (valid value) -> stays unchanged
  config.page ??= 1; // page is null -> becomes 1
  print("config after ??= : delay=${config.delay}, page=${config.page}");

  // [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript] Dart DOES NOT HAVE
  // the [||=] and [&&=] operators: Dart's [||] and [&&] only accept
  // [bool] values (as seen in point 1), and there is no assignment
  // shortcut for this case - the test must be written explicitly
  String displayedMessage = "";
  // explicit equivalent of [displayedMessage ||= "default message"]:
  // in Dart, you must write yourself the meaningful "false" test (here:
  // empty string) rather than relying on a generic notion of "false"
  if (displayedMessage.isEmpty) {
    displayedMessage = "default message";
  }
  print("displayedMessage after the if equivalent to ||= : $displayedMessage");

  // explicit equivalent of [a &&= b] (assigns b only if a is already
  // "true"): again, a simple if, [a] having to be a real boolean
  bool loggedInUser = true;
  if (loggedInUser) {
    loggedInUser = true; // the "b" of a &&= b
  }
  print("loggedInUser after the if equivalent to &&= : $loggedInUser");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 4) numeric separators [_] in literals
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] Dart does NOT accept the [_]
  // character as a visual separator in a numeric literal: "1_000_000"
  // is a syntax error in Dart. The number must be written "in full",
  // possibly formatting it for display with the [intl] package
  // (NumberFormat) if readability on display is the goal.
  const int oneMillion = 1000000;
  print("oneMillion = $oneMillion");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 5) BigInt
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] JavaScript's
  // [number] type is a double-precision float, which loses its
  // precision beyond about 2^53 - hence the need for a separate [BigInt]
  // type for very large exact integers (bank card numbers,
  // identifiers...). Dart's [int] type, on the other hand, is a REAL signed
  // 64-bit integer on all native platforms (VM, AOT): it remains
  // exact up to 2^63-1, well beyond JavaScript's [Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER]
  // (2^53-1) - most uses that would require a
  // BigInt in JavaScript therefore simply do not need one in Dart.
  print("the Dart equivalent of Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER does not exist: "
      "int is exact up to 9223372036854775807 (2^63-1)");
  const int bigNumber = 9007199254740993; // > 2^53, imprecise in JS, exact here
  print("bigNumber = $bigNumber (exact, whereas it would lose its "
      "precision stored in a JavaScript Number)");
  // for a truly unlimited need (beyond 64 bits, e.g. cryptographic
  // calculation), Dart does NOT offer a BigInt type in its
  // standard library (dart:core): you must then turn to a
  // third-party package such as package:fixnum, or implement your own calculation -
  // a much rarer need than in JavaScript, given the above.
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// utility classes for the optional chaining demonstration
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
class Address {
  final String city;
  Address({required this.city});
}

class PersonWithOptionalAddress {
  final String name;
  final Address? address; // address is optional (nullable)
  PersonWithOptionalAddress({required this.name, this.address});
}

class ObjectWithMethod {
  String sayHello() => "hello!";
}

class Configuration {
  int? delay;
  int? page;
  Configuration({this.delay, this.page});
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • [??] and [?.] (null coalescing, optional chaining) have been part of Dart for a long time and behave exactly as they do in TypeScript.
    • Line 63: [config.delay ??= 1000;]: The logical assignment [??=] exists in Dart, with the same syntax as in TypeScript.
    • Dart has no equivalent for the operators [||=] and [&&=]: its [||]/[&&] only accepts [bool], so there is no generic concept of “false” to bypass—a simple explicit [if] replaces them.
    • [1_000_000] is a SYNTAX ERROR in Dart: unlike TypeScript, no visual separators are allowed in a numeric literal.
    • [int] is a valid 64-bit integer EXACT SIGNED on any native Dart platform, up to 2^63-1 —well beyond [Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER] (2^53-1): most use cases that would require a JavaScript [BigInt] simply do not need them in Dart, which, incidentally, does not offer [BigInt] in its standard library.

    3.1.10. Conclusion

    This first section laid the groundwork: strict typing without implicit coercion, the distinction between [final] and [const], systematic block scope, and the absence of destructuring assignment (compensated for by Dart 3 patterns). These differences will come up throughout the course.

    3.2. Arrays

    In Dart, an “array” is called a [list] ([List]). This section covers classic list operations: reference vs. value, iteration, methods on the ends, functional methods, and the recent “immutable” methods of JavaScript.

    // arr_01.dart
// Ports arr-01.ts: a list is an object handled through its reference,
// exactly like a JavaScript/TypeScript array.
void main() {
  final List<int> arr1 = [1, 2, 3];
  // REFERENCE copy, not content copy
  final List<int> arr2 = arr1;
  // arr1 and arr2 point to the same list - [identical] is the Dart
  // equivalent of [===] applied to object IDENTITY (instead of [==], which for
  // Lists compares the content; see the remark below)
  print("identical(arr1, arr2) : ${identical(arr1, arr2)}");
  // the list can be modified through either arr1 or arr2
  arr2[1] = 10;
  print("arr1=$arr1");
  print("arr2=$arr2");

  // [Dart-specific remark] unlike JavaScript where [arr1 === arr2]
  // and [arr1 == arr2] are equivalent for arrays (reference comparison
  // in both cases), Dart's [==] operator on a List
  // object also compares the REFERENCE by default (not the content): []
  // == [] is therefore false in Dart, as the following line shows
  print("[1, 2] == [1, 2] (two different lists) : ${[1, 2] == [1, 2]}");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 7: [final List<int> arr2 = arr1;] copies the REFERENCE, not its contents: [arr1] and [arr2] refer to the same list, exactly as in JavaScript.
    • Line 11: [identical(arr1, arr2)] is the Dart equivalent of [===] applied to objects (IDENTITY test).
    • Line 22: [[1, 2] == [1, 2]] is FALSE in Dart: unlike JavaScript, where [===] and [] are equivalent on arrays (reference comparison in both cases), the Dart operator [] applied to a [List] ALSO compares, by default, the reference, not the content.

    // arr_02.dart
// Ports arr-02.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] a JavaScript
// array is "sparse": you can write arr[3] = 100 on an
// empty array, which automatically extends its length to 4, leaving
// "holes" (indexes without a value, different from undefined). A Dart
// List is NOT sparse: its valid indexes always go from 0 to length-1
// without holes, and writing arr[3] on a list of length 0 throws a
// [RangeError] (index out of bounds) - the list never grows by
// itself through indexed assignment. To grow, use [add] (at the end)
// or one of the methods of the next section (arr_03.dart, arr_04.dart).
void main() {
  // [dynamic] because this list will contain values of different types
  final List<dynamic> arr = [];
  print("arr=$arr, length=[${arr.length}]");
  print("-------------------------------");

  // no direct equivalent of arr[3] = 100 on an empty list: we build
  // the same visual result ("holes") by explicitly filling with
  // null up to the desired index, which makes the holes VISIBLE (nulls),
  // where JavaScript leaves them invisible (neither value, nor explicit
  // undefined)
  while (arr.length <= 3) {
    arr.add(null);
  }
  arr[3] = 100;
  arr[1] = "eight";
  print("arr=$arr, length=[${arr.length}]");
  print("-------------------------------");

  // toString
  print("arr.toString=[${arr.toString()}]");
  print("-------------------------------");

  // the keys of a Dart list are always 0..length-1: no separate [keys()]
  // method, the indexes are used directly with a [for]
  for (var key = 0; key < arr.length; key++) {
    print("key=[$key], value=[${arr[key]}]");
  }
  print("-------------------------------");

  // the values of the list - [arr] IS already the iterable of its values,
  // unlike JavaScript where arr.values() returns a separate iterator
  for (var value in arr) {
    print("value=[$value]");
  }
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • A Dart list is NEVER sparse: its valid indices always range from 0 to [length-1] without any gaps.
    • Line 10: Writing [arr[3]] to an empty list raises a [RangeError]—unlike JavaScript, where writing [arr[3] = 100] to an empty array automatically extends it by creating invisible “gaps.”
    • The script explicitly fills in values from [null] up to the desired index to recreate, VISIBLY, the same visual effect as the holes in JavaScript.
    • Line 45: [for (var value in arr)]: a Dart [List] that is already an iterable over its values—no need for a separate method like in JavaScript.

    // arr_03.dart
// Ports arr-03.ts: iterating over a list, and its manipulation methods
// at both ends (pop/push/shift/unshift) as well as splice.
void main() {
  // a list can contain different types of data
  final List<dynamic> arr = [
    1,
    2,
    "one",
    "two",
    true,
    [10, 20],
    {'prop1': 10, 'prop2': "abc"},
  ];
  // print can display the content of a list
  show(1);
  print("arr=$arr");
  show(2);
  // iterating over the list with forEach
  arr.forEach((element) {
    print("element=$element ${element.runtimeType}");
  });
  show("2b");
  // iterating with for-in, more idiomatic in Dart than forEach for a
  // simple iteration (forEach does not accept break/continue, for-in does)
  for (final element in arr) {
    print("element=$element ${element.runtimeType}");
  }
  show(3);
  // iterating over the list with a classic indexed for
  for (var i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    print("i=$i arr[i]=${arr[i]}");
  }
  show(4);
  // modification arr[i]
  arr[5] = [];
  print("arr=$arr");
  show(5);
  // we remove the last element of the list - removeLast() is
  // the Dart equivalent of pop()
  var element = arr.removeLast();
  print("element=$element arr=$arr");
  show(6);
  // we add an element at the end of the list - add() is the equivalent of
  // push() (for a single element)
  arr.add('xyz');
  print("arr=$arr");
  show(7);
  // we add an element at the beginning of the list - insert(0, ...) is
  // the equivalent of unshift()
  arr.insert(0, 1000);
  print("arr=$arr");
  show(8);
  // we remove the 1st element - removeAt(0) is the equivalent of shift()
  element = arr.removeAt(0);
  print("element=$element arr=$arr");
  show(9);
  // we remove element no. 2 from the list - there is no [splice]
  // method in Dart; we first retrieve the relevant subset with
  // [sublist], then remove it with [removeRange]
  var elements = arr.sublist(2, 3);
  arr.removeRange(2, 3);
  print("element(s)=$elements arr=$arr");
  show(10);
  // we remove two elements from the list starting at element no. 1
  elements = arr.sublist(1, 3);
  arr.removeRange(1, 3);
  print("element(s)=$elements arr=$arr");
}

// function
void show(Object param) {
  print("[$param :::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::"
      ":::::::::::::: ]");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • Line 20: [arr.forEach(...)] exists, but [for (final element in arr)] (line 26) is preferred in Dart for a simple loop: unlike [forEach], a [for-in] accepts both [break] and [continue].
    • Line 41: [arr.removeLast()] replaces [pop()]; [arr.add(...)] (line 46) replaces [push()] (for a single element); [arr.insert(0, ...)] (line 51) replaces [unshift()], and [arr.removeAt(0)] (line 55) replaces [shift()].
    • Dart does not have a method named [splice]: first, retrieve the relevant subset using [sublist], then remove it using [removeRange]—two steps instead of a single call.

    // arr_04.dart
// Ports arr-04.ts: the functional list manipulation methods -
// map, reduce, filter (where), find (firstWhere), findIndex (indexWhere),
// indexOf, lastIndexOf, sort.
void main() {
  // a list
  final List<int> arr = List.generate(10, (i) => i * 10);
  print("arr=$arr");

  // map - returns a (lazy) Iterable; .toList() materializes it as a list,
  // as JavaScript's .map() always does
  final arr2 = arr.map((element) => {'prop1': element, 'prop2': element * element}).toList();
  print("arr=$arr");
  print("arr2=$arr2");

  // reduce WITHOUT initial value - same signature as in JavaScript
  final sum = arr.reduce((accumulator, currentValue) => accumulator + currentValue);
  print("sum arr=$sum");

  // [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] Dart has no reduce() WITH an
  // initial value: that is the role of a separate method, [fold], whose
  // 1st parameter is precisely the initial value
  final sum2 = arr.fold(10, (accumulator, currentValue) => accumulator + currentValue);
  print("sum2 arr=$sum2");

  // filter -> where (returns an Iterable; .toList() to get a list)
  final arr4 = arr.where((element) => element > 50).toList();
  print("arr4=$arr4");

  // find -> firstWhere
  final element1 = arr.firstWhere((element) => element > 20);
  print("element1=$element1");

  // findIndex -> indexWhere
  final index1 = arr.indexWhere((element) => element == 20);
  print("index1 20=$index1");

  // indexOf - identical to JavaScript
  final index2 = arr.indexOf(30);
  print("index2 30=$index2");
  final index3 = arr.indexOf(31);
  print("index3 31=$index3");

  // lastIndexOf - identical to JavaScript
  final index4 = [4, 5, 4, 2].lastIndexOf(4);
  print("index4 4=$index4");

  // sort - [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] unlike JavaScript's
  // sort(), which returns the sorted array (in addition to modifying it in
  // place), Dart's sort() returns NOTHING (void): it only
  // modifies the list in place. So you must sort THEN read the list again.
  final arr5 = [4, 5, 4, 2];
  arr5.sort();
  print("arr5=$arr5");

  // reverse sort, with a comparator - same principle as in JavaScript: the
  // comparator returns a negative, zero, or positive number
  final arr6 = [4, 5, 4, 2];
  arr6.sort((e1, e2) {
    if (e1 > e2) {
      return -1;
    } else if (e1 == e2) {
      return 0;
    } else {
      return 1;
    }
  });
  print("arr6=$arr6");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • Line 12: [arr.map(...)] returns a LAZY [Iterable] (evaluated on demand)—[.toList()] materializes it as a list.
    • line 17: [arr.reduce(...)] (with no initial value) has the same signature as JavaScript.
    • [WARNING] Dart's [reduce] does NOT accept an initial value: this is the role of a separate method, [fold], whose first parameter is precisely this initial value.
    • [filter] -> [where], [find] -> [firstWhere], [findIndex] -> [indexWhere] - [where] returns, like [map], a lazy [Iterable].
    • Line 53: [WARNING] [arr5.sort()] returns NOTHING ([void]): unlike [sort()] from JavaScript, which returns the sorted array IN ADDITION to modifying it in place, Dart’s [sort()] simply modifies the list in place—you must sort, THEN re-read the list.

    // arr_05.dart
// Ports arr-05.ts.
// The original TypeScript script presented array methods
// ADDED to JavaScript between 2022 and 2023 (at, findLast, toSorted...).
// Dart did not follow exactly the same schedule of new features: some
// of these needs have long been covered (differently), others not
// at all. This script therefore shows, for each, the current Dart equivalent.
void main() {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 1) access to the last element: no [at(index)] method with a negative
  //    index in Dart, but dedicated shortcuts already exist
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  final List<int> arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];
  print("arr[arr.length - 1] = ${arr[arr.length - 1]}"); // works as in JS
  print("arr.last = ${arr.last}"); // -> last element, more readable (equivalent of at(-1))
  print("arr[arr.length - 2] = ${arr[arr.length - 2]}"); // no shortcut for the second-to-last
  print("arr.first = ${arr.first}"); // -> equivalent to arr[0] / arr.at(0)
  // no equivalent of "hello".at(-1) on String: we use
  // classic indexing
  const string = "hello";
  print("string[string.length - 1] = ${string[string.length - 1]}");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) findLast() and findLastIndex()
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // findLast() -> lastWhere(), which has always existed in Dart (not a
  // recent addition as in JavaScript)
  final List<int> numbers = [5, 12, 8, 21, 3, 17];
  final lastEven = numbers.lastWhere((n) => n % 2 == 0);
  print("last even number = $lastEven"); // -> 8

  // [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] Dart has no ready-made
  // findLastIndex(); we rebuild it with an explicit backwards loop
  var lastEvenIndex = -1;
  for (var i = numbers.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    if (numbers[i] % 2 == 0) {
      lastEvenIndex = i;
      break;
    }
  }
  print("index of the last even number = $lastEvenIndex");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) the "immutable" methods (toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with)
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // sort() and removeRange()/insert() (see arr_03.dart, arr_04.dart) modify
  // the list in place, exactly as in JavaScript.
  // [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] Dart does NOT offer dedicated
  // "to..." methods: the same result is obtained by copying the list
  // FIRST (with [List.of] or [[...original]]), then applying
  // the mutating operation to the COPY - the principle remains simple, just a
  // bit more explicit than in JavaScript.
  final List<Object> original = [4, 5, 4, 2];

  // toSorted -> copy, then sort the copy
  final sorted = List.of(original)..sort();
  print("original = $original (unchanged)");
  print("sorted = $sorted");

  // toReversed -> .reversed is already NON-MUTATING in Dart (it returns a
  // new lazy Iterable, unlike reverse(), which does not even exist
  // on List in Dart): .toList() materializes it
  final reversed = original.reversed.toList();
  print("reversed = $reversed, original still = $original");

  // toSpliced -> copy, then apply removeRange + insertAll to the copy
  final modified = List.of(original);
  modified.removeRange(1, 3);
  modified.insertAll(1, ["a", "b", "c"]);
  print("modified = $modified, original still = $original");

  // with(index, value) -> copy, then assign the index on the copy
  final replaced = List.of(original);
  replaced[0] = 999;
  print("replaced = $replaced, original still = $original");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // why it is useful: the same argument as in JavaScript applies in
  // Dart, notably with Flutter, where a [State] must never be modified
  // in place but replaced by a new state to trigger a new
  // display.
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 10: There is no [at(index)] method with a negative index in Dart, but dedicated shortcuts already exist: [arr.last] (equivalent to [at(-1)]) and [arr.first] (equivalent to [at(0)]).
    • [findLast] -> [lastWhere], which has always existed in Dart (not a recent addition like JavaScript). There is no ready-made equivalent for [findLastIndex]: an explicit reverse traversal reconstructs it.
    • [WARNING] Dart does not provide dedicated “immutable” methods ([toSorted], [toSpliced], [with]): you get the same result by copying the list ([List.of(original)]), then applying the MUTATING operation to the copy.
    • Line 63: [original.reversed] is an exception: it is already NON-MUTATING in Dart (it returns a new lazy [Iterable]), whereas Dart doesn’t even offer a mutant [reverse()] for [List].

    3.2.6. Conclusion

    Dart lists are manipulated using method names that often differ from their JavaScript equivalents ([removeLast] for [pop], [where] for [filter]...), but the same principles apply: shared references, multiple traversals, and the distinction between mutating and non-mutating operations.

    3.3. The objects

    Dart has no direct equivalent to the literal object JavaScript, whose properties can be freely created at any time. Depending on whether the object’s SHAPE is known in advance or not, this section uses either a [Map<String, dynamic>] (free form) or a true Dart class (fixed form)—a conscious choice that does not exist in TypeScript.

    // obj_01.dart
// Ports obj-01.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] a JavaScript
// object literal can receive NEW properties at any time
// (obj1.prop1 = "abcd"), which the TypeScript interface only announces
// in advance. A Dart class, on the other hand, has a set of fields FIXED at
// compile time: impossible to add a field to an instance afterwards.
// For an object whose properties are built dynamically (as
// here), the natural Dart equivalent is therefore a [Map<String, dynamic>], not
// a class.
void main() {
  // an empty Map, with dynamic properties ("keys")
  final Map<String, dynamic> obj1 = {};
  // the properties of the object can be created dynamically
  obj1['prop1'] = "abcd";
  print('obj1=$obj1');
  // another property
  obj1['prop2'] = [1, 2, 3];
  print("obj1=$obj1");
  // in Dart, there is only ONE notation to access a property
  // of a Map (the one with square brackets): no separate "dot"
  // notation (obj1.prop3) as in JavaScript, since precisely a Map
  // is not an object with fixed fields
  obj1['prop3'] = true;
  print("obj1=$obj1");

  // obj1 is a reference to the Map (like a pointer), not the Map
  // itself
  final Map<String, dynamic> obj2 = obj1;
  // obj2 and obj1 point to the same Map
  obj2['prop1'] = "xyzt";
  print("obj1=$obj1");
  print("obj2=$obj2");

  // keys can be variables
  const String var1 = 'prop1';
  print('prop1=${obj1[var1]}');
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 14: [Map<String, dynamic> obj1 = {};]: for an object whose properties are constructed dynamically, the natural Dart equivalent is a [Map], not a class—a Dart class has a set of fields FIXED at compile time.
    • line 16: [obj1['prop1'] = "abcd";]: there is only one notation for accessing a property of a [Map] (brackets) — no separate dot notation ([obj1.prop1]) as in JavaScript.
    • Line 30: [obj2 = obj1;] copies the REFERENCE: [obj1] and [obj2] refer to the same [Map], following exactly the same principle as for lists (see arr_01.dart).

    // obj_02.dart
// Ports obj-02.ts: a multi-level object.
//
// [difference with obj_01.dart] here, unlike obj-01, the SHAPE of
// the object is known and fixed in advance (first name, age, father, mother always
// present): this is exactly the case where Dart prefers a real class to
// a Map - safer (the compiler checks each field) and more readable
// (person.father.firstName rather than person['father']['firstName']).
import 'dart:convert';

class SubPerson {
  final String firstName;
  // not final: the script modifies the mother's age further down
  // (person.mother.age = 40), which requires a mutable field.
  int age;
  SubPerson({required this.firstName, required this.age});

  factory SubPerson.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) =>
      SubPerson(firstName: json['firstName'] as String, age: json['age'] as int);
  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() => {'firstName': firstName, 'age': age};
}

class PersonWithFamily {
  final String firstName;
  int age;
  final SubPerson father;
  SubPerson mother;
  PersonWithFamily({
    required this.firstName,
    required this.age,
    required this.father,
    required this.mother,
  });

  factory PersonWithFamily.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => PersonWithFamily(
        firstName: json['firstName'] as String,
        age: json['age'] as int,
        father: SubPerson.fromJson(json['father'] as Map<String, dynamic>),
        mother: SubPerson.fromJson(json['mother'] as Map<String, dynamic>),
      );
  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() =>
      {'firstName': firstName, 'age': age, 'father': father.toJson(), 'mother': mother.toJson()};

  @override
  String toString() => toJson().toString();
}

void main() {
  final person = PersonWithFamily(
    firstName: "martin",
    age: 12,
    father: SubPerson(firstName: "paul", age: 45),
    mother: SubPerson(firstName: "micheline", age: 42),
  );
  // accessing the properties
  print("person first name=${person.firstName}");
  print("mother first name=${person.mother.firstName}");
  person.mother.age = 40;
  print("mother age=${person.mother.age}");
  // print can display an object IF toString() has been defined (see above)
  // - unlike JavaScript's console.log, which inspects the structure
  // of an object even without a custom toString()
  print("person=$person");
  print("mother=${person.mother.toJson()}");

  // we can also display the jSON string of the object - jsonEncode/jsonDecode
  // (from the standard package dart:convert) are the Dart equivalents of
  // JSON.stringify/JSON.parse; they require the object to provide a
  // toJson() (see above), unlike JSON.stringify, which can
  // serialize any JavaScript object without configuration
  final String json = jsonEncode(person);
  print("jSON=$json");
  // the jSON can be read back - jsonDecode returns a generic
  // Map<String, dynamic> (not directly a PersonWithFamily): you must go
  // explicitly through fromJson again, unlike JSON.parse, which returns
  // a JavaScript object directly usable as is
  final PersonWithFamily person2 = PersonWithFamily.fromJson(jsonDecode(json));
  print("father=${person2.father.toJson()}");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • Since the object’s SHAPE is known and fixed in advance, this script prefers a real class to a [Map]—it’s safer (each field is checked at compile time) and more readable ([person.father.firstName] rather than [person['father']['firstName']]).
    • Line 71: [jsonEncode(person)]/[jsonDecode(json)] (line 77) (dart:convert) are equivalent to [JSON.stringify]/[JSON.parse], but require the class to provide a [toJson()] —unlike [JSON.stringify], which serializes any JavaScript object without configuration.
    • [jsonDecode] returns a generic [Map<String, dynamic>], never directly a [PersonWithFamily]: you must explicitly go through [fromJson], unlike [JSON.parse], which directly returns a JavaScript object that can be used as-is.
    • Line 63: [print("person=$person")] displays something useful ONLY because [toString()] has been redefined —unlike [console.log], which inspects an object’s structure even without a custom [toString()].

    // obj_03.dart
// Ports obj-03.ts: getters and setters.
// Here, a Dart getter/setter is defined exactly as in a TypeScript
// class ([get]/[set] keywords) - the only difference is that in Dart
// they necessarily live in a class (never in a Map).
class PersonWithName {
  String? _name;

  // getter
  String get name {
    print("name getter");
    return _name!;
  }

  // setter
  set name(String aName) {
    print("name setter");
    _name = aName;
  }
}

void main() {
  final person = PersonWithName();
  // setter
  person.name = "Hercule";
  // getter
  print(person.name);
  // [difference with TypeScript] the field [_name] is REALLY private here
  // (the [_] prefix is a real rule of the Dart language, applied at
  // the FILE/library level), whereas the [_name] of obj-03.ts
  // is only a naming convention: nothing prevented, in TypeScript,
  // writing person._name = "xyz" from outside the object. In Dart,
  // inside this same file, direct access remains possible (we
  // are in the same library):
  person._name = "xyz";
  print("person._name=${person._name}");
  // ... but from ANOTHER file that would import this class,
  // person._name would be inaccessible: only the get/set name pair
  // would remain usable. This point is taken up and developed
  // in classes/class_05.dart (truly private fields).
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • A Dart getter/setter is written using the same keywords: [get]/[set] as in TypeScript—the only difference is that they must be defined within a class, never in a [Map].
    • Line 7: [String? _name;]: the [_name] field is private here—the [_] prefix is a valid Dart rule (at the file/library level), whereas [_name] from TypeScript is merely a naming convention with no actual effect.
    • Line 35: [person._name = "xyz";] remains possible HERE within the same file (same library)—but would be inaccessible from ANOTHER file that imports this class (explored in detail in classes/class_05.dart).

    // obj_04.dart
// Ports obj-04.ts: property name notation and shorthand notation.
class FullName {
  final String lastName;
  final String firstName;
  const FullName({required this.lastName, required this.firstName});
}

void main() {
  // [difference with TypeScript] a Dart class has only ONE notation
  // for its fields (never surrounded by single or double quotes like
  // the properties of a JavaScript object literal): this point of the
  // original script therefore only applies to [Map]s, shown below.
  const obj1 = FullName(lastName: "martin", firstName: "jean");
  print("firstName=${obj1.firstName}");

  // on a Map, however, the key is always a character string,
  // surrounded by single or double quotes - there is no "literal"
  // notation like {lastName: "martin"} without quotes on a Dart Map
  final Map<String, String> obj2 = {'lastName': "martin", 'firstName': "jean"};
  print("lastName=${obj2['lastName']}");

  final Map<String, String> obj3 = {"lastName": "martin", "firstName": "jean"};
  // only one possible notation to access a Map key (square
  // brackets) - no separate "dot" notation (obj3.lastName)
  print("lastName=${obj3["lastName"]}");

  // [difference with TypeScript] Dart has no shorthand notation
  // equivalent to {obj1, obj2} to build a Map from variables
  // with the same name as the desired keys: the key must always be written
  // explicitly
  final obj4 = {'obj1': obj1, 'obj2': obj2};
  // obj1 will be displayed as "Instance of 'FullName'": without a custom
  // toString() (see obj_02.dart), Dart only displays the name of the
  // class, where JavaScript's console.log would have inspected every detail
  print("obj4=$obj4");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • A Dart class has only one notation for its fields—never enclosed in quotes—so this point in the original script boils down to ONE notation.
    • In a [Map], the key is always a string enclosed in quotes: there is no literal notation without quotes, such as [{lastName: "martin"}] in JavaScript.
    • Dart does not have a shorthand notation equivalent to [{obj1, obj2}] for constructing a [Map] from variables with the same names as the desired keys: you must always write the key explicitly.

    // obj_05.dart
// Ports obj-05.ts: an object can carry a method (toString).
import 'dart:convert';

class PersonWithToString {
  final String firstName;
  final int age;
  final Map<String, dynamic> father;
  final Map<String, dynamic> mother;

  PersonWithToString({
    required this.firstName,
    required this.age,
    required this.father,
    required this.mother,
  });

  // method - in Dart, overriding toString() is done with the
  // [override] keyword, which explicitly documents that we override a method
  // inherited from the [Object] class (the common ancestor of all Dart
  // classes) - there is no equivalent of this annotation in TypeScript
  @override
  String toString() => jsonEncode({
        'firstName': firstName,
        'age': age,
        'father': father,
        'mother': mother,
      });
}

void main() {
  final person = PersonWithToString(
    firstName: "martin",
    age: 12,
    father: {'firstName': "paul", 'age': 45},
    mother: {'firstName': "micheline", 'age': 42},
  );

  // usage - print() automatically calls toString(), as would
  // a string interpolation "$person"
  print("person=$person");
  print("person.toString=${person.toString()}");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • [@override String toString() => ...]: Redefining [toString()] is done using the keyword [@override], which explicitly documents that a method inherited from [Object] (the common ancestor of all Dart classes) is being redefined - There is no equivalent of this annotation in TypeScript.
    • Line 41: [print("person=$person")] automatically calls [toString()], just as any string interpolation in ["$person"] would.

    // obj_06.dart
// Ports obj-06.ts: dynamic iteration over the properties of an object.
//
// [difference with TypeScript] this script only makes sense, in Dart, for a
// [Map]: a Dart class has fixed fields, known at compile time, and
// therefore never needs to be "iterated over" dynamically like a JavaScript
// object. We go back here to a Map<String, dynamic>, as in obj_01.
void main() {
  final Map<String, dynamic> person = {
    'firstName': "martin",
    'age': 12,
    'father': {'firstName': "paul", 'age': 45},
    'mother': {'firstName': "micheline", 'age': 42},
  };

  print(person);
  print("-----------------------");

  // [difference with TypeScript] a Dart Map has no "prototype
  // chain" like a JavaScript object: ALL its keys are its
  // own, so there is no equivalent of the risk of
  // iterating over an INHERITED property (which hasOwnProperty avoids in
  // JavaScript). A simple for-in on .entries is enough, without any
  // additional test:
  for (final entry in person.entries) {
    print("${entry.key} = ${entry.value}");
  }

  // another equivalent syntax, with forEach
  print("-----------------------");
  person.forEach((key, value) {
    print("$key = $value");
  });

  // or again, if we only want the keys (equivalent of Object.keys)
  print("-----------------------");
  for (final key in person.keys) {
    print("$key = ${person[key]}");
  }
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 25: [for (final entry in person.entries)]: A Dart [Map] does not have a “prototype chain” like a JavaScript object—all its keys belong to it directly, so there is no equivalent to the risk of iterating over a INHERITED property (which [hasOwnProperty] avoids in JavaScript).
    • Line 31: [person.forEach((key, value) => ...)] and [person.keys] (line 37) (equivalent to [Object.keys]) offer the same traversals, with no additional testing required.

    // obj_07.dart
// Ports obj-07.ts: destructuring.
// [NEW, Dart 3] object destructuring ("object patterns") is a
// RECENT feature in Dart (3.0, 2023) - developed in the chapter
// Dart 3.x New features (dart3/patterns.dart). We use it here, ahead
// of that chapter, since it is the direct equivalent of what this
// TypeScript script does.
class FullName {
  final String lastName;
  final String firstName;
  const FullName({required this.lastName, required this.firstName});
}

void main() {
  const obj1 = FullName(lastName: "martin", firstName: "jean");

  // destructuring obj1 into the variables [n, p]: the syntax
  // [:lastName] means "extract the lastName field, and name it lastName"; it can
  // then be renamed with an [alias] as here
  final FullName(lastName: n, firstName: p) = obj1;
  print("n=$n p=$p");

  // [difference with TypeScript] the PARAMETERS of a Dart function do not
  // directly support writing a pattern (unlike
  // TypeScript, where function f({lastName, firstName}: FullName) destructures
  // directly in the parameter list). Destructuring must be done in
  // the BODY of the function, with a pattern variable declaration:
  void f(FullName obj) {
    final FullName(lastName: n2, firstName: p2) = obj;
    print("f-n2=$n2 f-p2=$p2");
  }

  f(obj1);

  // shorthand notation [:lastName] (equivalent to [lastName: lastName]) - the
  // pattern name directly becomes the name of the created variable, exactly
  // like TypeScript's shorthand notation {lastName, firstName}
  void h(FullName obj) {
    final FullName(:lastName, :firstName) = obj;
    print("h-lastName=$lastName h-firstName=$firstName");
  }

  h(obj1);
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 20: [final FullName(lastName: n, firstName: p) = obj1;]: object pattern extraction is a feature of Dart (3.0, 2023), used here ahead of the chapter on [Dart 3.x New Features] because it directly corresponds to what this TypeScript script does.
    • [WARNING] The PARAMETERS of a Dart function do NOT directly support a pattern—unlike TypeScript ([function f({lastName, firstName})]): you must use destructuring within the function’s BODY.
    • Line 39: [final FullName(:lastName, :firstName) = obj;]: The shorthand notation [:lastName] (equivalent to [lastName: lastName]) makes the field name directly the name of the created variable—the exact equivalent of the shorthand notation [{lastName, firstName}] for TypeScript.

    The result of execution is as follows:

    // obj_08.dart
// Ports obj-08.ts: shallow cloning with the spread operator.
void main() {
  // the spread operator [...] exists in Dart, but ONLY in a
  // collection literal (List, Set or Map) - never to "spread" the
  // fields of an arbitrary class instance (there is, by the way, no
  // notion of "enumerable fields" in Dart, unlike JavaScript).
  // On a Map, however, it behaves exactly as in JavaScript:
  final Map<String, String> obj1 = {'lastName': "martin", 'firstName': "jean"};

  // shallow clone of obj1 with the spread operator
  final Map<String, String> obj2 = {...obj1};

  // checks - identical() is the Dart equivalent of === applied to
  // object identity (see arr_01.dart); obj2 points to a COPY of obj1
  print("identical(obj1, obj2) : ${identical(obj1, obj2)}");
  print("obj2=$obj2");

  // -------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [Dart-specific complement] for a CLASS (rather than a Map), the Dart
  // idiom for clone-with-modifications is a hand-written [copyWith]
  // method (widely used with Flutter, to never modify a state
  // in place - see arr_05.dart):
  // -------------------------------------------------------------------
  final p1 = _FullName(lastName: "martin", firstName: "jean");
  final p2 = p1.copyWith(firstName: "paul"); // copy of p1, first name changed
  print("p1=$p1, p2=$p2");
}

class _FullName {
  final String lastName;
  final String firstName;
  const _FullName({required this.lastName, required this.firstName});

  _FullName copyWith({String? lastName, String? firstName}) =>
      _FullName(lastName: lastName ?? this.lastName, firstName: firstName ?? this.firstName);

  @override
  String toString() => '{lastName: $lastName, firstName: $firstName}';
}

    Let’s break down this code:

    • The spread operator [...] exists in Dart, but ONLY in a collection literal ([List], [Set], or [Map])—never to spread the fields of any class instance (Dart has no concept of “enumerable fields”).
    • Line 12: [{...obj1}] superficially clones a [Map], exactly as in JavaScript; [identical(obj1, obj2)] (line 16) confirms that [obj2] points to a COPY.
    • For a CLASS, the Dart idiom for “clone-with-modification” is a hand-written [copyWith] method (widely used with Flutter)—there is no generic equivalent of the spread operator for classes.

    The result of the execution is as follows:

p1={lastName: martin, firstName: jean}, p2={lastName: martin, firstName: paul}

    // obj_09.dart
// Ports obj-09.ts.
import 'dart:convert';

void main() {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 1) Object.hasOwn(object, property)
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [difference with TypeScript] as explained in obj_06.dart, a Dart Map
  // has no prototype chain: any key present in the Map
  // necessarily belongs to it as its "own". [containsKey] has therefore always
  // been the only test needed - there was no need to add a
  // late [Map.hasOwn] like JavaScript's [Object.hasOwn] of 2022.
  final Map<String, dynamic> person = {'lastName': "Dupont", 'firstName': "Jean"};

  print("person.containsKey('lastName') = ${person.containsKey('lastName')}");
  print("person.containsKey('age') = ${person.containsKey('age')}");

  // typical use in an iteration over properties
  print("-----------------------");
  for (final key in person.keys) {
    print("$key = ${person[key]}");
  }

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) deep cloning
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // obj_08.dart shows shallow cloning with the
  // spread operator [...obj] - but a spread only clones the 1st level: the
  // sub-Maps remain shared!
  final Map<String, dynamic> original = {
    'lastName': "Dupont",
    'address': {'city': "Nantes", 'postalCode': "44000"},
  };

  // shallow cloning with spread
  final Map<String, dynamic> shallowCopy = {...original};
  (shallowCopy['address'] as Map)['city'] = "Angers"; // also modifies the address of [original]!
  print("shallow copy modified the original : "
      "${(original['address'] as Map)['city'] == "Angers"}");

  // reset for the next test
  (original['address'] as Map)['city'] = "Nantes";

  // [difference with TypeScript] Dart has no native structuredClone()
  // function. For a structure made entirely of "JSON" types
  // (Map, List, String, num, bool, null - exactly the case here), the simplest
  // Dart idiom is a round trip through jsonEncode/jsonDecode:
  // this forces a complete copy, at every level
  final Map<String, dynamic> deepCopy = jsonDecode(jsonEncode(original));
  (deepCopy['address'] as Map)['city'] = "Angers";
  print("deep copy did not modify the original : "
      "${(original['address'] as Map)['city'] == "Nantes"}");
  print("original = $original");
  print("deepCopy = $deepCopy");
  // NB: this detour through jsonEncode/jsonDecode only works for
  // "JSON-serializable" data; to deep-clone an arbitrary
  // class, you must write your own cloning (e.g. a recursive
  // copyWith, see obj_08.dart), as Dart offers no generic equivalent.

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) optional chaining + nullish on nested accesses
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // a very frequent combination in practice to read a partial
  // configuration - identical to TypeScript, these two operators having existed in
  // Dart for a long time (see basics_09.dart)
  displayTheme(null);
  displayTheme({'appearance': {'theme': "dark"}});
  displayTheme({'appearance': <String, dynamic>{}});
  displayTheme(<String, dynamic>{});
}

void displayTheme(Map<String, dynamic>? configuration) {
  // if configuration, configuration['appearance'] or
  // configuration['appearance']['theme'] is missing, we fall back on "light"
  // without ever crashing
  final theme = (configuration?['appearance'] as Map?)?['theme'] ?? "light";
  print("theme = $theme");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 16: [person.containsKey('lastName')]: just like [Map], Dart has no prototype chain (see obj_06.dart), [containsKey] has always been the only necessary test—there’s no need for a later equivalent of the 2022 [Object.hasOwn] in JavaScript.
    • Line 50: [jsonDecode(jsonEncode(original))]: Dart does not have a native [structuredClone()] function. For a structure that is entirely “JSON” ([Map], [List], [String], [num], [bool], [null]), this round-trip forces a complete copy at all levels—unlike the superficial spread of obj_08.dart, which clones only the first level.
    • line 77: [configuration?['appearance'] as Map?)?['theme'] ?? "light"]: The optional chaining [?.]/[?[ ]] combined with [??] works exactly as in TypeScript; these two operators have long existed in Dart (see basics_09.dart).

    The result of the execution is as follows:

    3.3.10. Conclusion

    The choice between [Map] and a class is the central issue of this section: use [Map<String, dynamic>] for a free-form or unknown structure (such as an ordinary JavaScript object), and a class for a fixed structure verified by the compiler. Dart 3 patterns (obj_07.dart) already demonstrate that this choice does not prevent you from retaining most of the convenience of TypeScript destructuring.

    // str_01.dart
// Ports str-01.ts: strings are read-only.
void main() {
  // a string
  const String string1 = "abcd ";
  // type - runtimeType is the Dart equivalent of typeof
  print("string1.runtimeType=${string1.runtimeType}");
  // character no. 2 - [] indexing works as in TypeScript
  print("string1[2]=${string1[2]}");
  // causes an error: a Dart String, like a TypeScript string,
  // only offers [] indexing for READING. Unlike TypeScript, there
  // is not even a []= operator for String: the following line is
  // a COMPILATION error ("The operator '[]=' isn't defined for the
  // class 'String'"), whether or not one first tries to type it
  // dynamically.
  // string1[2] = "0";
}

    Let's discuss this code:

    • [string1[2]]: Bracket indexing works the same way as in TypeScript, but only for READING.
    • [WARNING] Dart doesn't even have an operator for [[]=] for [String]: [string1[2] = "0";] is a COMPILATION ERROR ([The operator '[]=' isn't defined for the class 'String']), whereas TypeScript simply results in a type error during write indexing.

    // str_02.dart
// Ports str-02.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] JavaScript has
// TWO ways of representing a string: the primitive type [string]
// (literal "xyzt"), and the object type [String] (built with [new
// String("xyzt")]), which is a real object, distinct from its value (`new
// String("a") === new String("a")` is actually false!). Dart has
// only ONE [String] type: there is no separate "boxed object" variant
// to compare with the primitive type. This script is therefore shorter than
// the original; the only common point shown is that toString (here Dart only has
// "length") works the same in all cases.
void main() {
  // a string literal
  const String string1 = "abcd ";
  print("string1.runtimeType=${string1.runtimeType}");

  // no equivalent of "new String(...)": an explicitly built string
  // remains the same String type, with the same value
  final String string2 = String.fromCharCodes("xyzt".codeUnits);
  print("string2.runtimeType=${string2.runtimeType}");

  // another syntax (without new) - still the same type
  const String string3 = "12 34";
  print("string3.runtimeType=${string3.runtimeType}");

  // lengths behave identically in all cases,
  // since in Dart this is one and the same type
  print("string1.length=${string1.length}");
  print("string2.length=${string2.length}");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • Dart has only ONE string type: no distinction between a primitive type [string] and an object type [String] constructed with [new String(...)], as in JavaScript.
    • Line 20: [String.fromCharCodes(...)] explicitly constructs a string, but remains the same, unique type [String], with the same value—there is no equivalent to the trap [new String("a") === new String("a")] (false in JavaScript).

// Ports str-03.ts: string interpolation and extraction of a substring.
void main() {
  const String string = "Introduction to Dart by example";
  // Dart has, like TypeScript, native string interpolation (no
  // third-party library needed) - with $variable or ${expression}
  // (unlike TypeScript, which reserves `` for templates and keeps ""
  // or '' for simple strings, $"..." Dart always accepts $/${})
  //
  // [difference with TypeScript] substr(start, length) is an OLD,
  // deprecated JavaScript method (deprecated well before
  // TypeScript uses it here, to stay faithful to the original script).
  // Dart never had it: its equivalent is substring(start, end) - the
  // 2nd parameter is an END position, not a LENGTH.
  final String str =
      "[$string].substring(3, 5)=" + string.substring(3, 5); // 2 characters starting at no. 3
  print(str);
}

    Let’s break down this code:

    • String interpolation ([$variable], [${expression}]) is native to Dart, as is TypeScript, but works with ["..."] and ['...'] interchangeably—there is no reserved [...] syntax as in JavaScript.
    • Line 16: [string.substring(3, 5)]: Dart has never had a [substr(start, length)] (deprecated method of JavaScript)—its equivalent is [substring(start, end)], whose second parameter is an END position, not a LENGTH.

    // str_05.dart
// Ports str-05.ts: the classic sprintf format specifiers.
import 'dart:convert';
import 'package:sprintf/sprintf.dart';

void main() {
  const String string = "Dart";
  // character strings
  print(sprintf("[%s, %%s]=>[%s]", [string, string]));
  print(sprintf("[%s, %%20s]=>[%20s]", [string, string]));
  print(sprintf("[%s, %%-20s]=>[%-20s]", [string, string]));
  // integers
  print(sprintf("[%d, %%d]=>[%d]", [10, 10]));
  print(sprintf("[%d, %%4d]=>[%4d]", [10, 10]));
  print(sprintf("[%d, %%-4d]=>[%-4d]", [10, 10]));
  print(sprintf("[%d, %%04d]=>[%04d]", [10, 10]));
  // reals
  print(sprintf("[%f, %%f]=>[%f]", [-10.5, -10.5]));
  print(sprintf("[%f, %%10.2f]=>[%10.2f]", [-10.5, -10.5]));
  print(sprintf("[%f, %%-10.2f]=>[%-10.2f]", [-10.5, -10.5]));
  print(sprintf("[%f, %%010.3f]=>[%010.3f]", [-10.5, -10.5]));

  // [difference with TypeScript] the npm package [sprintf-js] adds
  // JavaScript-specific specifiers, absent from the "classic" sprintf:
  // %j (JSON), %T (type), %t (boolean). The Dart package [sprintf] only
  // supports the standard C/POSIX specifiers (%s, %d, %f...) - we
  // get the same result for %j and %T with the equivalent Dart
  // tools (jsonEncode, runtimeType), combined with %s:
  final person = {'name': "mathieu", 'age': 34};
  // json (equivalent of sprintf-js's %j)
  print(sprintf("person (%%j equivalent)=%s", [jsonEncode(person)]));
  // type (equivalent of sprintf-js's %T)
  print(sprintf("person type (%%T equivalent)=%s", [person.runtimeType]));
  // boolean (equivalent of sprintf-js's %t - %s is enough, a Dart bool
  // is already displayed as "true"/"false", exactly the expected format)
  print(sprintf("boolean (%%t equivalent)=%s", [4 == 4]));
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • The standard C/POSIX format specifiers ([%s], [%d], [%f], width, alignment, leading zeros) work exactly like their [sprintf-js] equivalents.
    • [WARNING]: The Dart package [sprintf] does NOT include the extensions specific to [sprintf-js] ([%j], [%T], [%t]): the same result is obtained by combining [%s] with the equivalent Dart tools—[jsonEncode] for [%j], [.runtimeType] for [%T], and a simple Boolean (already shown as [true]/[false]) for [%t].
