    // str_06.dart
// Ports str-06.ts: the usual string manipulation methods.
import 'package:sprintf/sprintf.dart';

void main() {
  const String string = "  Introduction to Dart ";
  // substring(10, 12): 2 characters starting at no. 10 (substring(start,
  // end), not substr(start, length) - see str_03.dart)
  print(sprintf("[%s].substring(10,12)=[%s]", [string, string.substring(10, 12)]));
  // trim: removal of leading and trailing blanks - identical to
  // TypeScript
  print(sprintf("[%s].trim()=[%s]", [string, string.trim()]));
  // toLowerCase: conversion to lowercase
  print(sprintf("[%s].toLowerCase=[%s]", [string, string.toLowerCase()]));
  // toUpperCase: conversion to uppercase
  print(sprintf("[%s].toUpperCase=[%s]", [string, string.toUpperCase()]));
  // indexOf: position of a searched string in the string, -1 if absent
  print(sprintf("[%s].indexOf('Dart')=[%s]", [string, string.indexOf('Dart')]));
  print(sprintf("[%s].trim().indexOf('abcd')=[%s]", [string, string.indexOf('abcd')]));
  // includes -> contains: true if the searched string is in the string
  print(sprintf("[%s].contains('Dart')=[%s]", [string, string.contains('Dart')]));
  // length: length of the string - a property, as in TypeScript
  print(sprintf("[%s].length=[%s]", [string, string.length]));
  // slice(7,10) -> substring(7,10): the same parameters (start, end) have
  // exactly the same meaning here as in slice, unlike substr (see
  // str_03.dart)
  print(sprintf("[%s].substring(7,10)=[%s]", [string, string.substring(7, 10)]));
  // match: RegExp.firstMatch(string) is the Dart equivalent of
  // string.match(/regexp/) - "intro" in uppercase or lowercase
  // (caseSensitive: false is the equivalent of the /i/ flag)
  final RegExp pattern = RegExp('intro', caseSensitive: false);
  print(sprintf("[%s].match(intro,i)=[%s]", [string, pattern.firstMatch(string)?.group(0)]));
  // replace: replaces string1 with string2 in string
  // replaceFirst: only replaces the 1st occurrence of i with x
  print(sprintf("[%s].replaceFirst('i','x')=[%s]", [string, string.replaceFirst('i', 'x')]));
  // [difference with TypeScript] replaceAll ALREADY REPLACES ALL the
  // occurrences in Dart, and always has (no need for a regular
  // expression with a /g/ flag like the replace(/i/g,'x') of str-06.ts, nor
  // to wait for ECMAScript 2021 as in plain JavaScript - see str_07.dart)
  print(sprintf("[%s].replaceAll('i','x')=[%s]", [string, string.replaceAll('i', 'x')]));
  // split: splits the string into words separated by the split parameter -
  // returns the list of these words
  // RegExp(r'\s*'): words separated by 0 or more spaces
  print(sprintf("[%s].split(RegExp(r'\\s*'))=[%s]", [string, string.split(RegExp(r'\s*'))]));
  // RegExp(r'\s+'): words separated by one or more spaces
  print(sprintf("[%s].split(RegExp(r'\\s+'))=[%s]", [string, string.split(RegExp(r'\s+'))]));
}

    Let’s break down this code:

    • line 9: [string.substring(10, 12)], [.trim()], [.toLowerCase()] (line 14), [.toUpperCase()] (line 16), [.indexOf(...)], [.length] (line 23) behave like their equivalents TypeScript.
    • Line 21: [string.contains('Dart')] replaces [includes]; [string.substring(7, 10)] (line 27) replaces [slice(7, 10)]—the parameters (start, end) have exactly the same meaning here as in [slice], unlike in [substr].
    • Lines 31–32: [RegExp('intro', caseSensitive: false).firstMatch(string)]: the Dart equivalent of [string.match(/regexp/i)], with the [caseSensitive: false] option serving the same purpose as the [/i/] flag.
    • Line 40: [WARNING] [string.replaceAll('i', 'x')] ALREADY replaces ALL the occurrences in Dart, and this has always been the case—no need for a regular expression with a flag like JavaScript's [/g/], nor to wait for a recent version of the language (see str_07.dart).

    // str_07.dart
// Ports str-07.ts.
void main() {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 1) replaceAll(search, replace)
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [difference with TypeScript] as noted in str_06.dart, replaceAll()
  // already replaces ALL the occurrences in Dart, without this ever having
  // required an addition to the language (unlike ECMAScript 2021, where
  // this method had to be added to avoid the detour through a
  // regular expression with the /g/ flag)
  const String string = "one cat, two cats, three cats";
  print("replaceFirst (only 1 occurrence) : ${string.replaceFirst("cat", "dog")}");
  print("replaceAll (all the occurrences) : ${string.replaceAll("cat", "dog")}");
  // replaceAll also accepts a regular expression (without needing
  // any particular flag, unlike JavaScript's mandatory /g/)
  print("replaceAll with regexp : ${string.replaceAll(RegExp('cat'), "dog")}");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) allMatches(string) - the Dart equivalent, present from the start, of
  //    matchAll() added to JavaScript in 2020
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  const String text = "Jean is 30 years old, Marie is 25 years old, Paul is 40 years old";
  final RegExp pattern = RegExp(r'(\w+) is (\d+) years old');

  // allMatches returns an Iterable<RegExpMatch>, each giving access to the
  // captured groups AND to their position - exactly like matchAll()
  print("-----------------------");
  for (final result in pattern.allMatches(text)) {
    print("name = ${result.group(1)}, age = ${result.group(2)}, "
        "position = ${result.start}");
  }

  // the Iterable can be turned into a List with .toList()
  final allResults = pattern.allMatches(text).toList();
  print("number of matches = ${allResults.length}");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) isWellFormed() / toWellFormed()
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [difference with TypeScript] Dart has no direct equivalent of these
  // two ECMAScript 2024 methods. A Dart String is, like a JavaScript
  // string, a sequence of UTF-16 code units (the same isolated "half-
  // characters" are therefore theoretically possible), but the
  // problem arises much less often in practice: Dart strings
  // almost always come from an already validated UTF-8 decoding (.dart
  // source files, dart:convert.utf8.decode...), which precisely rejects
  // malformed sequences at the source, rather than letting through an
  // invalid character as a naive split can do in
  // JavaScript. The closest everyday Dart concern, by the way, is
  // not "well formed in the UTF-16 sense" but "a single displayed
  // character (grapheme) can take up SEVERAL code units" (emoji,
  // combined accents...) - a different subject, handled by the
  // [characters] package (pub.dev/packages/characters), outside the scope of this
  // script.
  const String validString = "café ☕";
  print("validString.runes.length (number of code points) = "
      "${validString.runes.length}");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • [string.replaceAll(...)] also accepts a regular expression without requiring any specific flags—confirming the point raised in str_06.dart.
    • [pattern.allMatches(text)] is the Dart equivalent, available ALWAYS, of [matchAll()], added to JavaScript in 2020: it returns a [Iterable<RegExpMatch>], each providing access to the captured groups AND their respective positions.
    • [WARNING] Dart has no direct equivalent to [isWellFormed()]/[toWellFormed()] (ECMAScript 2024): this issue arises much less frequently in practice, as Dart strings almost always originate from a previously validated UTF-8 decoding—see the comment at the top of the file for the distinction regarding the [characters] package.

    3.4.9. Conclusion

    Manipulating Dart strings is similar to their TypeScript equivalents, with method names that are sometimes different ([substring] instead of [substr]/[slice], [contains] instead of [includes]), and a consistent absence of the pitfalls associated with recent changes in JavaScript ([replaceAll], [matchAll]), as Dart made these choices from the outset.

    3.5. Regular expressions

    The syntax of regular expressions itself is identical to that of JavaScript (Dart uses, like JavaScript, the PCRE/ECMA-262 syntax): only the API for using them from within the code changes.

    // regexp_01.dart
// Ports regexp-01.ts: regular expressions in Dart - retrieving the
// different fields of a string with captured groups.
void main() {
  // the pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
  // we only want to retrieve the sequence of digits - the syntax of
  // regular expressions itself is identical to JavaScript's
  // (Dart uses, like JavaScript, the PCRE/ECMA-262 syntax)
  RegExp pattern = RegExp(r'(\d+)');
  print("type of a regular expression : ${pattern.runtimeType}");
  // we match the string against the pattern
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "xyz1234abcd");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "12 34");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "abcd");

  // the pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
  // we want the sequence of digits as well as the fields that follow and precede it
  pattern = RegExp(r'^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$');
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "xyz1234abcd");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "12 34");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "abcd");

  // the pattern - a date in dd/mm/yy format
  pattern = RegExp(r'^\s*(\d\d)/(\d\d)/(\d\d)\s*$');
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "10/05/97");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "  04/04/01  ");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "5/1/01");

  // the pattern - a decimal number
  pattern = RegExp(r'^\s*([+|-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*$');
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "187.8");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "-0.6");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "4");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, ".6");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "4.");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, " + 4");
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
void comparePatternToString(RegExp pattern, String string) {
  // compares the string [string] to the pattern [pattern]
  print("----------- string=$string, pattern=$pattern");
  // [difference with TypeScript] Dart has only ONE method to obtain
  // the first detailed result (captured groups): [firstMatch] - there
  // is no distinction between a RegExp-side method (exec) and a
  // String-side method (match) as in JavaScript, the Dart API being
  // organized solely around RegExp
  final RegExpMatch? result = pattern.firstMatch(string);
  if (result == null) {
    print("comparison with firstMatch= no match");
  } else {
    // rebuilds the list of groups, like the array returned by exec()
    final groups = List.generate(
      result.groupCount + 1,
      (i) => result.group(i),
    );
    print("comparison with firstMatch= $groups (position=${result.start})");
  }
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • Line 9: [RegExp(r'(\d+)')]: The template syntax is identical to JavaScript; the prefix [r] (RAW string) avoids having to double the backslashes, an added convenience unique to Dart.
    • Line 48: [pattern.firstMatch(string)]: Dart has only one method for obtaining the first detailed result—there is no distinction, as in JavaScript, between a method on the [RegExp] side ([exec]) and a method on the [String] side ([match]), as Dart is organized solely around [RegExp].
    • Line 55: [result.group(i)]/[result.groupCount] (line 54) reconstruct the list of captured groups, like the array returned by [exec()].

    3.5.3. Conclusion

    Regular expressions are written the same way in Dart and in TypeScript; only the API used to process them ([firstMatch], [allMatches], [hasMatch], all three supported by [RegExp]) differs, in a more consistent manner than in JavaScript.

    // func_01.dart
// Ports func-01.ts: how parameters are passed to a function.
// The general principle is the same as in TypeScript: a "primitive" type
// (int, String, bool - immutable) SEEMS passed by value (modifying it in
// the function does not change the caller's variable), while a mutable
// object (List, Map, class instance) is passed by REFERENCE (
// modifying it in the function IS visible to the caller). In reality, Dart
// (like JavaScript) ALWAYS passes the reference itself by value: what
// changes is only that reassigning the local PARAMETER (param =
// something else) never affects the caller's variable, whereas
// MODIFYING the pointed object (param.push(...), param[i] = ...) always
// affects it, if that object is mutable.
void main() {
  // ----------------------- number - seems passed by value (immutable)
  // [WARNING, difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] a Dart nested function
  // can NOT reference a local variable declared further down in
  // the same block, even if the call happens after that declaration: unlike
  // JavaScript, where the scope of a closure is resolved at runtime, Dart
  // requires the variable to be already declared at the point where the compiler reads
  // the reference. We therefore declare [count] BEFORE the function that uses it.
  int count = 10;
  void doSomethingWithNumber(int param) {
    param++;
    print("[param inside function]=$param [type]=${param.runtimeType} "
        "[same variable as the caller]=${identical(param, count)}");
  }

  doSomethingWithNumber(count);
  print("[count outside function]=$count");

  // --------------------- string - seems passed by value (immutable)
  void doSomethingWithString(String param) {
    param += " xyz";
    print("[param inside function]=$param [type]=${param.runtimeType}");
  }

  String text = "abcd";
  doSomethingWithString(text);
  print("[text outside function]=$text");

  // --------------------- boolean - seems passed by value (immutable)
  void doSomethingWithBoolean(bool param) {
    param = !param;
    print("[param inside function]=$param [type]=${param.runtimeType}");
  }

  bool boolean = true;
  doSomethingWithBoolean(boolean);
  print("boolean [outside function]=$boolean");

  // --------------------- list - passed by reference (mutable)
  // same remark as above: [arr] is declared before the function that
  // references it in its body.
  final List<int> arr = [10, 20, 30];
  void doSomethingWithList(List<int> param) {
    param.add(1000);
    print("[param inside function]=$param [type]=${param.runtimeType} "
        "[same list as the caller]=${identical(param, arr)}");
  }

  doSomethingWithList(arr);
  print("[arr outside function]=$arr");

  // --------------------- object (Map) - passed by reference (mutable)
  // same remark as above: [obj] is declared before the function that
  // references it in its body.
  final Map<String, dynamic> obj = {};
  void doSomethingWithMap(Map<String, dynamic> param) {
    param['aNewProperty'] = "xyz";
    print("[param inside function]=$param [type]=${param.runtimeType} "
        "[same Map as the caller]=${identical(param, obj)}");
  }

  doSomethingWithMap(obj);
  print("[obj outside function]=$obj");

  // --------------------- function
  // [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] a JavaScript
  // function IS an object: new properties can be dynamically assigned
  // to it (f.aNewProperty = "xyz"), which is what the
  // original script does. A Dart function IS NOT an extensible object: it
  // is impossible to attach a property to a variable of function
  // type. What IS possible, and achieves a comparable result
  // (remembering a state associated with a function), is a CLOSURE
  // in other words, a function that "captures" an outer variable.
  int callCounter = 0;
  int Function() f = () {
    callCounter++; // captures [callCounter] by reference
    return callCounter;
  };
  print("f() = ${f()}, callCounter = $callCounter");
  print("f() = ${f()}, callCounter = $callCounter");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • The general principle is the same as in TypeScript: an immutable type ([int], [String], [bool]) SEEMS passed by value, a mutable object ([List], [Map], class instance) is passed by REFERENCE.
    • Line 58: [identical(param, arr)] confirms that [param], within the function, refers to the same list as [arr] in the caller—modify [param] ([.add(...)] (line 56)) IS visible to the caller.
    • [WARNING] a JavaScript function IS an object, extensible with new properties; a Dart function IS NOT. The Dart equivalent for storing a state associated with a function is a CLOSURE: the variable [callCounter] is captured BY REFERENCE by the function [f].

    // func_02.dart
// Ports func-02.ts: a function can be assigned to a variable.
void main() {
  // an anonymous function can be assigned to a variable - the syntax of the
  // type [int Function(int, int)] reads "a function that takes two ints
  // and returns an int", the Dart equivalent of the arrow signature
  // [(a: number, b: number) => number] in TypeScript
  int Function(int, int) variable1 = (a, b) {
    return a + b;
  };
  print("variable1.runtimeType=${variable1.runtimeType}");
  // the variable is then used like a function
  print("variable1(10,12)=${variable1(10, 12)}");

  // in Dart, a function with a { ... } body can also be written with an
  // arrow [=>] IF its body is a single expression - the arrow
  // syntax is therefore, as in TypeScript, just a shorthand
  int Function(int, int, int) variable2 = (a, b, c) {
    return a - b + c;
  };
  print("variable2(10,12,14)=${variable2(10, 12, 14)}");

  // shorthand with =>, when there is only one expression in the
  // code of the function - this expression is then the return value
  int Function(int, int, int) variable3 = (a, b, c) => a + b + c;
  print("variable3(10,12,14)=${variable3(10, 12, 14)}");
}

    Let's comment on this code:

    • lines 8–10: [int Function(int, int) variable1 = (a, b) { ... };]: the notation [ReturnType Function(parameters)] describes the type of a function—the Dart equivalent of the arrow signature [(a: number, b: number) => number] for TypeScript.
    • line 25: [(a, b, c) => a + b + c]: The arrow syntax exists in Dart whenever a function has only a single expression as its body—exactly the same principle as in TypeScript.

    // func_03.dart
// Ports func-03.ts: a function can receive a function as a parameter.
void main() {
  // function g with a function f as parameter - the type [int Function(int,
  // int)] denotes the type of a function, exactly like the signature
  // [(a: number, b: number) => number] in TypeScript
  int g(int param1, int param2, int Function(int, int) f) {
    return f(param1, param2) + 100;
  }

  // uses of g
  print(g(0, 10, f1));
  print(g(0, 10, f2));
  // the actual parameter of function type can be passed directly -
  // arrow notation
  print(g(0, 10, (param1, param2) {
    return param1 + param2 + 30;
  }));
  // or, equivalently, with the body between braces
  print(g(0, 10, (param1, param2) {
    return param1 + param2 + 40;
  }));
}

// function f1
int f1(int param1, int param2) {
  return param1 + param2 + 10;
}

// function f2
int f2(int param1, int param2) {
  return param1 + param2 + 20;
}

    • [g(0, 10, (param1, param2) { ... })]: An actual parameter of type function can be passed directly in literal notation, with or without curly braces—as in TypeScript.

    // func_04.dart
// Ports func-04.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] in JavaScript,
// a function IS an object: properties can be assigned to it after the
// fact (f.prop1 = ...), and a function used with [new] plays the role
// of a constructor, [this] denoting the newly created object. A Dart
// function is NEVER an extensible object (see func_01.dart) and therefore cannot
// play this role. The Dart idiom that comes closest is
// the exact opposite: a CLASS whose INSTANCES behave like
// functions, thanks to a special method named [call] - this is called a
// "callable class".
void main() {
  // a "callable class" equivalent to the function f of the original script:
  // [f] carries a state (prop1), instead of receiving it from the outside after the
  // fact
  final f = _WithStateAndDisplay("val1");
  // f(...) actually calls f.call(...) - Dart automatically translates
  // "instance(arguments)" into "instance.call(arguments)"
  f.show();

  // a class g which, like a JavaScript constructor, initializes its
  // own state - this is exactly the normal role of a Dart
  // CONSTRUCTOR, no trick needed here at all: "new (g as any)()" in
  // TypeScript is just a classic Dart constructor
  final g = _LikeAClass();
  g.show();
}

class _WithStateAndDisplay {
  final String prop1;
  const _WithStateAndDisplay(this.prop1);

  // special method [call]: an instance of this class can be
  // "called" like a function (here without parameters, a bit like
  // "f()" would in JavaScript once show is attached to f)
  void call() => show();

  void show() => print(prop1);
}

class _LikeAClass {
  final String prop2 = "val2";
  void show() => print(prop2);
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 37: [void call() => show();]: the special method [call] makes an INSTANCE callable as a function ([f()] automatically becomes [f.call()])—this is the “callable class,” the Dart idiom closest to a JavaScript object function.
    • [_LikeAClass]: Unlike a constructor JavaScript (a function called with [new]), a Dart constructor requires no special tricks—that is its normal role.

    // func_05.dart
// Ports func-05.ts (the "rest" operator ...otherArgs).
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Dart has NO
// "rest" operator allowing an arbitrary number of surplus
// POSITIONAL arguments to be gathered into a list (unlike
// (arg1, ...otherArgs) in TypeScript). The caller must therefore explicitly
// build and pass a list, rather than "spreading" its arguments
// individually at the end of the call.
void main() {
  // call - we gather "the other arguments" into a list ourselves
  // [dynamic] (they are of different types here, as in the original
  // script)
  f(1, ["two", "three", {'x': 2, 'y': 3}]);
}

void f(int arg1, List<dynamic> otherArgs) {
  // 1st argument
  print("arg1=$arg1");
  // the other arguments
  var i = 0;
  for (final element in otherArgs) {
    print("otherArguments[$i]=$element");
    i++;
  }
}

// [addition] for a variable number of NAMED (rather than
// positional) parameters, Dart does offer a real dedicated mechanism: the
// optional named parameters, between braces - void f2({int? a, int?
// b}) - but these must be DECLARED one by one in the signature
// (so their number is not arbitrary either, unlike a rest
// operator).

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 14: [f(1, ["two", "three", {...}]);]: Dart has NO “rest” operator to group an arbitrary number of arguments ([...otherArgs])—the caller must construct and pass the list themselves.
    • Additionally (not shown in this script), Dart provides a true mechanism for a variable number of NAMED parameters—optional named parameters enclosed in curly braces—but these must be declared one by one in the signature.

    3.6.7. Conclusion

    The typing of Dart functions ([ReturnType Function(parameters)]) is very similar to the arrow function signatures of TypeScript. The fundamental difference lies elsewhere: a Dart function is never an extensible object, which rules out an entire set of JavaScript patterns (function-with-properties, constructor function, rest operator) in favor of Dart-specific equivalents (closures, callable classes, named parameters).

    // excep_01.dart
// Ports excep-01.ts: the try / catch / finally principle.
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

void main() {
  final DateFormat formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");
  for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    // date - time of the current moment
    final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
    // time formatting to get the milliseconds
    final String time = formatter.format(now);
    // the milliseconds
    final int milli = now.millisecond;
    // display
    print("--------------------iteration no. $i at $time");
    try {
      // random number (here, derived from the current milliseconds)
      final int number = milli % 2;
      if (number == 0) {
        // throw an error msg - in Dart, [throw] can throw any
        // object, exactly as in JavaScript (see excep_02.dart)
        throw "error";
      }
      // if we get here, there was no error
      print("no error");
    } catch (error) {
      // if we get here, there was an error
      print("error1=$error");
    } finally {
      // executed in all cases, error or not
      print("finally");
    }
  }
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • lines 16–23: [try { ... } catch (error) { ... } finally { ... }]: the same mechanism, with the same syntax, as in TypeScript.
    • Line 22: [throw "error";]: [throw] can throw ANY object in Dart, exactly as in JavaScript (explained in more detail in excep_02.dart).
    • Line 3: [import 'package:intl/intl.dart';]/[DateFormat] (line 6) provide the date formatting used to vary the example from one iteration to the next—the Dart equivalent of [moment.js] (already encountered in the TypeScript course).

    // excep_02.dart
// Ports excep-02.ts: we can "throw" just about anything
// to signal an error - true in Dart as in JavaScript.
void main() {
  var i = 0;
  print("--------------------attempt no. $i");
  // throw a character string
  try {
    throw "error msg";
  } catch (error) {
    // there was an error
    print("error=[$error], type=${error.runtimeType}");
  }

  // throw a list
  i++;
  print("--------------------attempt no. $i");
  try {
    throw [1, 2, 3];
  } catch (error) {
    print("error=[$error], type=${error.runtimeType}");
  }

  // throw a Map
  i++;
  print("--------------------attempt no. $i");
  try {
    throw {'name': "hercule", 'country': "ancient greece"};
  } catch (error) {
    print("error=[$error], type=${error.runtimeType}");
  }

  // throw an Exception - dart:core provides [Exception], the
  // idiomatic way to signal a "normal" (recoverable) error, the analogue
  // of the JavaScript [Error] used in the original script
  i++;
  print("--------------------attempt no. $i");
  try {
    throw Exception("network connection error");
  } catch (error) {
    print("error=[$error], type=${error.runtimeType}");
  }

  // same error, but reading its message directly
  i++;
  print("--------------------attempt no. $i");
  try {
    throw Exception("network connection error");
  } catch (error) {
    // the message is in [error.message] - unlike TypeScript where
    // the type of a catch variable is [unknown] by default, [catch
    // (error)] without an explicit type in Dart already types [error] as
    // [Object], without having to write [catch (error as any)];
    // but accessing .message still requires knowing that it is
    // an Exception (here we know it, see throw above)
    if (error is Exception) {
      print("error.toString=[$error], type(error)=${error.runtimeType}");
    }
  }
}

    Let’s break down this code:

    • line 9: [throw "error msg";], [throw [1, 2, 3];] (line 19), [throw {...};] (line 28): a string, a list, and a [Map] can all be thrown as-is - Dart does not restrict the type of the thrown object, such as JavaScript.
    • [throw Exception("...")]: [Exception] (dart:core) is the idiomatic way to signal a “normal” (recoverable) error, analogous to [Error] and JavaScript.
    • Line 49: [catch (error)] without an explicit type; [error] is already of type [Object] - Unlike TypeScript, where the type of a variable [catch] is [unknown] (line 51) by default and requires explicit type casting to be used.

    // excep_03.dart
// Ports excep-03.ts: differentiating the type of error received in a [catch].
void main() {
  // differentiate the type of error received in a [catch]
  for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
    final int milli = now.millisecond;
    print("--------------------iteration no. $i");
    try {
      // random number (derived from the current milliseconds)
      final int number = milli % 3;
      // Dart already has, in dart:core, several ready-to-use error types
      // comparable to JavaScript's ReferenceError/RangeError/EvalError
      // namely [StateError], [RangeError], [FormatException]
      switch (number) {
        case 0:
          throw StateError("error 1");
        case 1:
          throw RangeError("error 2");
        default:
          throw const FormatException("error 3");
      }
    } catch (error) {
      // there was an error - [is] is the Dart equivalent of [instanceof]
      if (error is StateError) {
        print("StateError : ${error.message}");
      } else if (error is RangeError) {
        print("RangeError : ${error.message}");
      } else if (error is FormatException) {
        print("FormatException : ${error.message}");
      }
    }
  }
}

    // excep_04.dart
// Ports excep-04.ts (the [cause] property of an error, ECMAScript 2022) and
// custom error classes.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Dart does NOT
// offer a standard [cause] field on its error classes
// (dart:core Exception/Error do not have one). To attach an original
// error to a new error (the same need as in 2022 on the
// JavaScript side), you must add it YOURSELF as an ordinary field of your
// own exception class - which is what this script does.

// it is common to catch a technical (low-level) error and to
// rethrow it as a more explicit (high-level) error

void readConfiguration() {
  // simulates a low-level technical error (e.g.: file not found)
  throw Exception("ENOENT: file 'config.json' not found");
}

// custom error class with a home-made [cause] field - we implement
// [Exception] (the marker interface of dart:core), as
// "extends Error" would on the TypeScript side
class StartupError implements Exception {
  final String message;
  final Object? cause;
  const StartupError(this.message, {this.cause});

  @override
  String toString() => "StartupError: $message";
}

void startApplication() {
  try {
    readConfiguration();
  } catch (technicalError) {
    // the named parameter [cause] makes it possible to attach the original error to
    // the new error, without losing the information
    throw StartupError("unable to start the application", cause: technicalError);
  }
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// another custom error class, with an additional business field
// (fieldInError) - always possible in Dart, without
// any particular notion of "language version" (unlike
// TypeScript, which dates this practice to 2015 via ES2015 classes)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
class ValidationError implements Exception {
  final String message;
  final String fieldInError;
  const ValidationError(this.message, this.fieldInError);

  @override
  String toString() => "ValidationError: $message";
}

bool validate(Object? age) {
  if (age is! int) {
    throw const ValidationError("the age must be a number", "age");
  }
  if (age < 0 || age > 130) {
    throw const ValidationError("the age must be between 0 and 130", "age");
  }
  return true;
}

void main() {
  try {
    startApplication();
  } catch (error) {
    if (error is StartupError) {
      print("error=${error.message}");
      // error.cause gives access to the original error, very useful for
      // debugging
      print("cause=${error.cause}");
    }
  }

  // some attempts with different values
  for (final Object? value in [25, -5, "thirty", 200]) {
    try {
      validate(value);
      print("value [$value] : validation OK");
    } catch (error) {
      // we can distinguish our business errors from the other errors thanks to [is]
      if (error is ValidationError) {
        print("value [$value] : validation error on "
            "[${error.fieldInError}] - ${error.message}");
      } else {
        // an unexpected error, not anticipated by our code
        rethrow;
      }
    }
  }
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 23: [class StartupError implements Exception]: Implementing [Exception] (the marker interface from dart:core) acts as [extends Error] in TypeScript.
    • Line 5: [WARNING] Dart does not provide the standard [cause] field on its error classes (unlike ECMAScript 2022): The [cause] field of [StartupError] is written manually, like a regular field of the class.
    • Line 48: [class ValidationError implements Exception] with a business field [fieldInError]: this has always been possible in Dart, without needing to know any specific “language version.”
    • Line 91: [rethrow;]: rethrows the captured error as-is when it is not of the expected type, to prevent an unexpected error from being silently swallowed.

    3.7.6. Conclusion

    Dart’s exception handling adopts the [try]/[catch]/[finally] triplet from TypeScript exactly as is. Two key points to note: the implicit [Object] type of an unannotated [catch] (more convenient than the [unknown] of TypeScript), and the absence of a standard [cause] field, which you’ll need to recreate yourself when the need arises.

    3.8. The modules

    ES and TypeScript modules distinguish a DEFAULT export (one per module, importable under any name) from NAMED exports (multiple per module). Dart does not make this distinction: any top-level declaration in a [.dart] file is automatically exported under its own name. The three [export-01/02/03.ts] scripts from the TypeScript course therefore boil down, in Dart, to a single file, [module_data.dart], imported in three different ways by the following three scripts.

    // module_data.dart
// Ports, on its own, the three scripts export-01.ts / export-02.ts /
// export-03.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] ES modules
// distinguish a "default export" (only one per module, importable under
// any name) and "named exports" (several per module,
// imported by their exact name, possibly renamed with [as]). Dart does NOT have
// this distinction: EVERY top-level declaration (class, function,
// variable) of a .dart file IS automatically exported, and always
// under its own name - there is no notion of an anonymous "default export"
// in Dart. The three variants of the original TypeScript script
// (anonymous default export, named default export, multiple named
// exports) therefore boil down, in Dart, to this one and same file.
class Module {
  final int data;
  const Module(this.data);

  void doSomething() {
    print(data);
  }
}

// a top-level instance, playing the role of the anonymous default export of the
// export-01.ts script
const Module data = Module(2);

// a top-level function, playing the role of the 2nd named export of
// export-03.ts
void doSomething() {
  print("doSomething");
}

    Let’s break down this code:

    • line 26: [const Module data = Module(2);] acts as the default export (ANONYMOUS) for [export-01.ts]; [void doSomething() { ... }] serves as the second named export for [export-03.ts].
    • In Dart, there is no concept of an anonymous “default export”: every top-level declaration is exported under its own name.

    // remote_config.dart
// Ports remote-config.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Dart DOES NOT HAVE
// "top-level await": it is impossible to use [await] at the top
// level of a .dart file, outside any function. This script therefore cannot,
// like its TypeScript equivalent, itself run an asynchronous
// call as soon as it is loaded and directly export the already resolved
// RESULT: instead it exposes an asynchronous FUNCTION, which the
// calling code (import_04.dart) will have to explicitly await with [await].
// This is, by the way, how async/async_06.dart already worked,
// BEFORE ECMAScript 2022 introduced top-level await on the
// JavaScript side - Dart never needed to depart from it, an explicit async
// function being enough for all cases.
class Configuration {
  final String applicationName;
  final String version;
  const Configuration({required this.applicationName, required this.version});

  @override
  String toString() => '{applicationName: $applicationName, version: $version}';
}

// a function that simulates an asynchronous call (e.g.: reading a remote
// configuration file)
Future<Configuration> loadFromNetwork() async {
  print("[remote_config] loading the configuration...");
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 300));
  print("[remote_config] configuration loaded");
  return const Configuration(applicationName: "Dart course", version: "2026");
}

    Let's break down this code:

    • Line 4: [WARNING] Dart does not support "top-level await": it is NOT possible to use [await] at the top level of a file, outside of any function.
    • Lines 26–31: [Future<Configuration> loadFromNetwork() async { ... }] therefore exposes an asynchronous FUNCTION to be explicitly awaited, rather than executing the call as soon as the file is loaded and directly exporting the resolved result.

    // import_04.dart
// Ports import-04.ts.
// As explained in remote_config.dart, Dart has no top-level
// await: the main program of a Dart script is ALWAYS the function
// [main], which you just need to declare [async] to be able to use [await] in it
// - exactly the role that an explicit "main" function already played in
// JavaScript before 2022 (see async/async_06.dart).
import 'remote_config.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  print("[import_04] before calling loadFromNetwork()");

  // unlike the original TypeScript script, where the IMPORT itself
  // triggered the loading (top-level await HIDDEN in
  // remote-config.js), here the wait is explicit and VISIBLE at the call:
  final Configuration configuration = await loadFromNetwork();

  print("[import_04] after the call: the configuration is already available");
  print("configuration = $configuration");

  // we can of course use [await] normally in [main], since
  // it is declared [async] above
  print("[import_04] waiting 200ms...");
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 200));
  print("[import_04] finished");
}

    • Line 16: [final Configuration configuration = await loadFromNetwork();]: the await is explicit and VISIBLE, unlike the HIDDEN top-level await in the import of the original TypeScript script.

    3.8.6. Conclusion

    The Dart module system is simpler than that of TypeScript: there is no distinction between default exports and named exports, and there is a single import mechanism (which may be prefixed and filtered by [show]/[hide]). The trade-off for this simplicity is the absence of top-level await, which requires exposing explicit asynchronous functions rather than values that are already resolved at load time.

    // async_01.dart
// Ports async-01.ts: the principle of an asynchronous action with a timer.
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

void main() {
  // start
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the script], ${time()}");

  // Timer (dart:core, via dart:async) is the Dart equivalent of setTimeout:
  // it arms a 1000 ms timer and immediately returns a [Timer] object
  // (the equivalent of the timer number returned by setTimeout); when the delay
  // has elapsed, the Dart runtime places the function in the
  // microtask/event queue, exactly as Node.js would
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    // this code will be executed when the timer has reached the value 0
    print("[end of the asynchronous action Timer], ${time(scriptStart)}");
  });

  // will be displayed before the msg of the timer's inner function
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

// utility displaying time and duration
String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • Lines 18–21: [Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () { ... })] (dart:async) is the Dart equivalent of [setTimeout]: it starts a timer and immediately returns a [Timer] object (the equivalent of the timer number returned by [setTimeout]).
    • Line 24: The message [[end of the main code of the script]] is displayed BEFORE the timer’s message: Dart is, like JavaScript, single-threaded for user code execution—the callback function for [Timer] is queued only after the main code has finished.

    // async_02.dart
// Ports async-02.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Node.js has a
// generic [EventEmitter] class, to which handlers are subscribed
// by any event NAME (character string). Dart has no
// direct equivalent in dart:async: the Dart idiom for a stream
// of events is a [Stream] (possibly "broadcast", to allow
// several subscribers), one per event CATEGORY rather than a generic
// emitter multiplexing string names. Here we create two
// StreamControllers, one for each "named event" of the original script.
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

void main() {
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the script], ${time()}");

  // two single-event "event emitters" - the equivalent, put
  // end to end, of eventEmitter.on('timer1Success', ...) and
  // eventEmitter.on('timer1Failure', ...)
  final StreamController<Map<String, int>> timer1Success = StreamController.broadcast();
  final StreamController<Map<String, int>> timer1Failure = StreamController.broadcast();

  // we subscribe to the [timer1Success] evt - .listen() is the equivalent of .on()
  timer1Success.stream.listen((result) {
    print("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [$result], "
        "${time(scriptStart)}, via the [timer1Success] stream");
  });

  // we subscribe to the [timer1Failure] evt
  timer1Failure.stream.listen((result) {
    print("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [$result], "
        "${time(scriptStart)}, via the [timer1Failure] stream");
  });

  // Timer arms a 1000 ms timer and immediately returns control
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    print("[Timer, end of the 1 s timer], ${time(scriptStart)}");
    // we emit an event to say that a result is available
    timer1Success.add({'success': 4});
    // we emit another event to say that another result is available
    timer1Failure.add({'failure': 6});
  });

  // will be displayed before the msgs of the events emitted by the function associated
  // with the timer
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • lines 24–25: [StreamController<Map<String, int>>.broadcast()] is the Dart idiom for an event stream —one [Stream] per event CATEGORY, rather than a generic emitter multiplexing string names like Node.js's [EventEmitter].
    • Line 28: [timer1Success.stream.listen((result) => ...)]: [.listen()] is equivalent to [.on(...)]; [.add(...)] (based on [StreamController], not [Stream]) triggers an event equivalent to [eventEmitter.emit(...)].

    // async_03.dart
// Ports async-03.ts: takes up async_02.dart again, adding costly SYNCHRONOUS
// code between arming the timer and the end of the main code -
// exactly as in JavaScript, this code blocks the execution of the timer
// (Dart is, like JavaScript, single-threaded as far as the execution
// of "user" code is concerned: a long synchronous loop delays by as much the
// processing of Timers and Streams, which only run once the
// call stack is back at rest).
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

void main() {
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the script], ${time()}");

  final StreamController<Map<String, int>> timer1Success = StreamController.broadcast();
  final StreamController<Map<String, int>> timer1Failure = StreamController.broadcast();

  timer1Success.stream.listen((result) {
    print("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [$result], "
        "${time(scriptStart)}, via the [timer1Success] stream");
  });
  timer1Failure.stream.listen((result) {
    print("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [$result], "
        "${time(scriptStart)}, via the [timer1Failure] stream");
  });

  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    print("[Timer, end of the 1 s timer], ${time(scriptStart)}");
    timer1Success.add({'success': 4});
    timer1Failure.add({'failure': 6});
  });

  // somewhat intensive synchronous code, which prevents the main code from
  // finishing before the end of the timer
  for (var i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
    for (var j = 0; j < 10000; j++) {
      i + i ^ 2 + i ^ 3;
    }
  }

  // will be displayed before the msgs of the events emitted by the function associated
  // with the timer
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

    Let’s break down this code:

    • A costly synchronous double loop, inserted between the timer being set and the end of the main code, delays the processing of [Timer] and [Stream]—a direct consequence of Dart’s single-threaded nature, as previously mentioned in async_01.dart.

    3.9.4. The Future Mechanism

    [Future<T>] is the Dart class equivalent to [Promise<T>]: an object that represents the result—which may not yet be available—of an asynchronous operation. Whereas TypeScript constructs a [Promise] using a [executor] passed directly to the constructor ([resolve]/[reject]), Dart separates this construction into a separate class, [Completer<T>]: [completer.complete(value)] serves as [resolve], [completer.completeError(error)] acts as [reject], and [completer.future] provides access to [Future] itself, to be distributed to anyone who wishes to receive the result.

    // async_04.dart
// Ports async-04.ts: getting the result of an asynchronous action without
// explicitly going through events, thanks to a [Future] - the Dart class
// equivalent to [Promise], which also implicitly uses
// events behind the scenes.
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

void main() {
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");

  // definition of an asynchronous task using a Future - built
  // with [Completer], the Dart class that plays the role of the "executor"
  // (resolve, reject) passed to the Promise constructor in JavaScript
  final DateTime future1Start = DateTime.now();
  final Completer<String> completer1 = Completer<String>();
  print("[start of the asynchronous function of future1], ${time(future1Start)}");
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    // this code is executed after a 1 second delay
    print("[end of the asynchronous function of future1], ${time(future1Start)}");
    // the asynchronous task returns a result with [complete] - the Future is
    // then successful (the Dart equivalent of [resolve])
    completer1.complete('[success]');
  });
  final Future<String> future1 = completer1.future;

  // we can know the result of the Future [future1] once it has
  // finished (successfully or in error) - .then() subscribes to success,
  // .catchError() to failure, .whenComplete() is executed in all cases
  // (the equivalent of then/catch/finally of the Promise class)
  future1
      .then((result) {
    print("[future1.then], ${time(future1Start)}, result=$result");
  }).catchError((result) {
    print("[future1.catchError], ${time(future1Start)}, result=$result");
  }).whenComplete(() {
    print("[future1.whenComplete] ${time(future1Start)}");
  });

  // definition of a second asynchronous task
  final DateTime future2Start = DateTime.now();
  final Completer<String> completer2 = Completer<String>();
  print("[start of the asynchronous function of future2], ${time(future2Start)}");
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 2000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous function of future2], ${time(future2Start)}");
    // the asynchronous task returns an error with [completeError] -
    // the Dart equivalent of [reject]
    completer2.completeError('[failure]');
  });
  final Future<String> future2 = completer2.future;

  future2.then((result) {
    print("[future2.then], ${time(future2Start)}, result=$result");
  }).catchError((result) {
    print("[future2.catchError], ${time(future2Start)}, result=$result");
  }).whenComplete(() {
    print("[future2.whenComplete], ${time(future2Start)}");
  });

  // will be displayed before the msgs of the asynchronous functions and of the
  // associated futures
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 19: [Completer<String> completer1 = Completer<String>();]: the Dart class that acts as the [executor] ([resolve]/[reject]) passed to the [Promise] constructor in JavaScript.
    • Line 26: [completer1.complete('[success]');]/[completer2.completeError('[failure]');] (line 51): the Dart equivalent of [resolve]/[reject].
    • [future1.then(...).catchError(...).whenComplete(...)]: the same sequence as [then]/[catch]/[finally] from a [Promise] TypeScript, with the same method names except for [whenComplete] (equivalent to [finally]).

    // async_05.dart
// Ports async-05.ts: [async] functions that return a [Future], and
// [Future.wait] - the Dart equivalent of [Promise.all].
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

// shape of the result returned by async01 and async02
class AsyncResult {
  final List<int> prop1;
  final String prop2;
  final int prop3;
  const AsyncResult(this.prop1, this.prop2, this.prop3);
  @override
  String toString() => '{prop1: $prop1, prop2: $prop2, prop3: $prop3}';
}

// an asynchronous function can return a Future and then have the keyword
// [async] - exactly as in TypeScript, except that here the [Future] is
// built with a [Completer] rather than an "executor" passed to the
// constructor (see async_04.dart)
Future<AsyncResult> async01(int p1) async {
  final Completer<AsyncResult> completer = Completer();
  print("[start of the asynchronous task async01]");
  final DateTime async01Start = DateTime.now();
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous task async01], ${time(async01Start)}");
    completer.complete(AsyncResult([10, 20, 30], "abcd", p1));
  });
  return completer.future;
}

Future<AsyncResult> async02(int p1, int p2) async {
  final Completer<AsyncResult> completer = Completer();
  print("[start of the asynchronous task async02]");
  final DateTime async02Start = DateTime.now();
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 2000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous task async02], ${time(async02Start)}");
    completer.complete(AsyncResult([11, 21, 31], "xyzt", p1 + p2));
  });
  return completer.future;
}

void main() {
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the script], ${time()}");

  // we launch the two asynchronous functions in parallel and wait
  // until both have finished - Future.wait only completes
  // if ALL succeed (like Promise.all), and fails as soon as one of the
  // two fails
  Future.wait([async01(10), async02(10, 20)]).then((result) {
    // the result is a List [result1, result2]
    print("[future-wait success], ${time(scriptStart)}, result=$result");
  }).catchError((error) {
    print("[future-wait error], ${time(scriptStart)}, error=$error");
  }).whenComplete(() {
    print("[future-wait whenComplete], ${time(scriptStart)}");
  });

  // will be displayed before the msgs of the asynchronous functions and of the
  // associated futures
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • lines 23–28: [Future<AsyncResult> async01(int p1) async { ... }]: an asynchronous function can be declared as [async] and return a [Future<T>], just like in TypeScript — except that here, the [Future] is constructed with an internal [Completer] rather than a [executor] passed to the constructor.
    • Line 53: [Future.wait([async01(10), async02(10, 20)])] is the Dart equivalent of [Promise.all]: it terminates only if ALL the tasks succeed, and fails as soon as any one of them fails.

    // async_06.dart
// Ports async-06.ts: parallel or sequential execution of several
// asynchronous tasks with async / await - a syntax practically
// identical to TypeScript's.
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

class AsyncResult {
  final List<int> prop1;
  final String prop2;
  const AsyncResult(this.prop1, this.prop2);
  @override
  String toString() => '{prop1: $prop1, prop2: $prop2}';
}

// an asynchronous function returning a Future
Future<AsyncResult> async01(DateTime async01Start) async {
  final Completer<AsyncResult> completer = Completer();
  print("[start of the asynchronous function async01], ${time()}");
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous function async01], ${time(async01Start)}");
    completer.complete(const AsyncResult([11, 21, 31], "abcd"));
  });
  return completer.future;
}

Future<AsyncResult> async02(DateTime async02Start) async {
  print("[start of the asynchronous function async02], ${time()}");
  final Completer<AsyncResult> completer = Completer();
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 2000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous function async02], ${time(async02Start)}");
    completer.complete(const AsyncResult([12, 22, 32], "xyzt"));
  });
  return completer.future;
}

Future<AsyncResult> async03(DateTime async03Start) async {
  print("[start of the asynchronous function async03], ${time()}");
  final Completer<AsyncResult> completer = Completer();
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 3000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous function async03], ${time(async03Start)}");
    // the asynchronous action fails - completeError() is the Dart equivalent
    // of reject()
    completer.completeError(const AsyncResult([13, 23, 33], "failure"));
  });
  return completer.future;
}

// asynchronous function - using async / await, syntax identical to
// TypeScript
Future<void> runSequentiallyAndInParallel() async {
  final DateTime sequentialStart = DateTime.now();
  print("------------ sequential execution of the asynchronous tasks started "
      "------------------------");
  try {
    // execution of [async01], waiting for it
    final DateTime async01Start = DateTime.now();
    final result1 = await async01(async01Start);
    print("[async01 result]=$result1");
    // execution of [async02], waiting for it
    final DateTime async02Start = DateTime.now();
    print("start async02-------------${time()}");
    final result2 = await async02(async02Start);
    print("[async02 result]=$result2");
    // execution of [async03], waiting for it
    final DateTime async03Start = DateTime.now();
    print("start async03-------------${time()}");
    final result3 = await async03(async03Start);
    print("[async03 result]=$result3");
  } catch (error) {
    // one of the asynchronous actions failed
    print("[sequential error]= $error, ${time(sequentialStart)}");
  } finally {
    print("[end of the sequential execution of the asynchronous tasks], ${time(sequentialStart)}");
  }

  final DateTime parallelStart = DateTime.now();
  print("------------ parallel execution of the asynchronous tasks started "
      "------------------------");
  try {
    final result = await Future.wait([
      async01(parallelStart),
      async02(parallelStart),
      async03(parallelStart),
    ]);
    print("[parallel success], ${time(parallelStart)}, result=$result");
  } catch (error) {
    print("[parallel error], ${time(parallelStart)}, error=$error");
  } finally {
    print("[end of the parallel execution of the asynchronous tasks], ${time(parallelStart)}");
  }

  print("[end of the function runSequentiallyAndInParallel], "
      "${time(sequentialStart)}");
}

void main() {
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the main code of the script], ${time()}");

  // [difference with TypeScript] just like "main();" in TypeScript,
  // which runs an async function WITHOUT waiting for it (it continues in
  // the background), the Dart call below does exactly the same thing:
  // runSequentiallyAndInParallel() is indeed launched, but [main]
  // does not wait for it (no [await] here) - the behaviour is therefore
  // identical
  runSequentiallyAndInParallel();

  // will be displayed before the various msgs of the asynchronous functions and of
  // their futures
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • The syntax [async]/[await] is virtually identical to TypeScript: [final result1 = await async01(async01Start);] suspends execution until [Future] is resolved.
    • Line 46: [completer.completeError(...)] within [async03] triggers an exception that is caught by the enclosing [try]/[catch], - the same behavior as a rejected [Promise] when encountering a [try]/[catch] around a [await].
    • Line 109: [runSequentiallyAndInParallel();] is called WITHOUT [await] from [main]: just like [main();] in TypeScript, the function is indeed launched but [main] does not wait for it—the same behavior, with no difference to note here.

    // async_07.dart
// Ports async-07.ts (additions to the Promise class). Dart has a direct
// equivalent for some of these additions (Completer, Future.any - with
// a different semantics, see below), but not for others
// (allSettled, the "real" any that waits for a first SUCCESS): this script
// rebuilds them by hand, which is also an opportunity to better understand
// what these methods really do.
import 'dart:async';

// small utility function: returns a Future that succeeds or fails
// after [delay]
Future<String> task(String name, int delayMs, bool succeeds) {
  final Completer<String> completer = Completer();
  Timer(Duration(milliseconds: delayMs), () {
    if (succeeds) {
      completer.complete("result of $name");
    } else {
      completer.completeError("failure of $name");
    }
  });
  return completer.future;
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) the equivalent of Promise.allSettled()
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] Dart's Future.wait(), like
// Promise.all(), GIVES UP at the first error (by default): we lose
// the result of the other Futures which, for their part, would have succeeded. There is
// no Future.allSettled() in dart:async; we rebuild it by
// "capturing" each error BEFORE gathering them with Future.wait (which,
// this way, never sees an error any more: each Future we give it
// always succeeds, with a "success" or "failure" result)
class Result<T> {
  final bool succeeded;
  final T? value;
  final Object? error;
  Result.success(this.value)
      : succeeded = true,
        error = null;
  Result.failure(this.error)
      : succeeded = false,
        value = null;
}

Future<Result<T>> _capture<T>(Future<T> future) {
  return future.then((v) => Result<T>.success(v)).catchError((e) => Result<T>.failure(e));
}

Future<void> demoAllSettled() async {
  print("--- equivalent of Promise.allSettled ---");
  final results = await Future.wait([
    _capture(task("task1", 300, true)),
    _capture(task("task2", 200, false)),
    _capture(task("task3", 100, true)),
  ]);
  for (var i = 0; i < results.length; i++) {
    final r = results[i];
    if (r.succeeded) {
      print("task${i + 1} succeeded : ${r.value}");
    } else {
      print("task${i + 1} failed : ${r.error}");
    }
  }
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) the equivalent of Promise.any()
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript] Future.any() EXISTS in
// Dart, but with a semantics DIFFERENT from Promise.any(): Future.any()
// completes with the FIRST result, whether it is a success OR
// an error (a kind of raw "race"), whereas Promise.any()
// specifically waits for a first SUCCESS, ignoring failures as long
// as at least one is still in the race. To reproduce the JavaScript
// behaviour, you have to write it yourself, with a Completer and a
// failure counter:
Future<String> promiseAny(List<Future<String>> futures) {
  final Completer<String> result = Completer();
  var failureCount = 0;
  final errors = List<Object?>.filled(futures.length, null);
  for (var i = 0; i < futures.length; i++) {
    futures[i].then((value) {
      if (!result.isCompleted) {
        result.complete(value);
      }
    }).catchError((error) {
      errors[i] = error;
      failureCount++;
      if (failureCount == futures.length && !result.isCompleted) {
        // all the tasks failed
        result.completeError(errors);
      }
    });
  }
  return result.future;
}

Future<void> demoAny() async {
  print("--- equivalent of Promise.any ---");
  try {
    final result = await promiseAny([
      task("slow-mirror", 500, true),
      task("fast-mirror", 100, true),
      task("broken-mirror", 50, false),
    ]);
    print("first available mirror : $result");
  } catch (globalError) {
    // globalError contains the list of all the individual errors
    print("all the mirrors failed : $globalError");
  }
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 3) the equivalent of Promise.withResolvers()
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// [difference with TypeScript] Dart did not need to wait until 2024 to
// have this feature: the [Completer] class, seen throughout
// this WHOLE async chapter (see async_04.dart and following), does exactly
// what Promise.withResolvers() does - "taking out" the
// resolve/reject functions (here .complete/.completeError) from the constructor, from
// the start, without an artificial intermediate variable.
Future<String> demoCompleter() {
  print("--- Completer (native, long-standing equivalent of "
      "Promise.withResolvers) ---");
  final Completer<String> completer = Completer();

  // we can resolve the Future from anywhere, for example in another
  // callback
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 200), () {
    print("[external callback] we trigger the resolution of the Future");
    completer.complete("value passed from an external callback");
  });

  return completer.future;
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 4) cancelling an asynchronous operation
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// [difference with TypeScript] Dart has no generic AbortController
// in dart:core/dart:async (the http package, for its part, offers its own
// approach - see the chapter "Dart's HTTP functions"). We can
// reproduce the same principle with a simple Completer playing the role of the
// cancellation signal, raced against the task itself thanks to
// Future.any() - which, here, is perfectly suitable: we precisely want the
// FIRST result, whether it is the normal end of the task or
// the cancellation (see the remark in point 2 above).
Future<String> cancellableTask(int delayMs, Future<void> cancellationSignal) {
  final Completer<String> completer = Completer();
  final Timer timer = Timer(Duration(milliseconds: delayMs), () {
    if (!completer.isCompleted) {
      completer.complete("finished normally");
    }
  });
  // if the cancellation signal is triggered first, we stop everything and
  // complete with an error
  cancellationSignal.then((_) {
    timer.cancel();
    if (!completer.isCompleted) {
      completer.completeError(Exception("operation cancelled"));
    }
  });
  return completer.future;
}

Future<void> demoCancellation() async {
  print("--- cancellation with a Completer used as a signal ---");
  final Completer<void> cancellationSignal = Completer();
  // we schedule the cancellation in 100 ms, before the normal end of the
  // task (500 ms)
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 100), () => cancellationSignal.complete());
  try {
    final result = await cancellableTask(500, cancellationSignal.future);
    print("result = $result");
  } catch (error) {
    print("error : $error");
  }
}

// successive execution of the demonstrations
Future<void> main() async {
  await demoAllSettled();
  await demoAny();
  print("--- Completer, result --- ${await demoCompleter()}");
  await demoCancellation();
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • [WARNING] Dart has NO [Future.allSettled]: [Future.wait], just like [Promise.all], GIVES UP at the first error—the class [Result<T>] and the function [_capture] rebuild the equivalent by capturing each error BEFORE combining the [Future]s with [Future.wait].
    • Line 70: [WARNING, key difference] [Future.any()] EXISTS in Dart but with a DIFFERENT SEMANTICS from [Promise.any()]: [Future.any()] returns the FIRST result (success OR error), whereas [Promise.any()] specifically waits for a first SUCCESS while ignoring failures—[promiseAny()] recreates this behavior manually, using a [Completer] and a failure counter.
    • [Completer] has always natively served the role of [Promise.withResolvers()] (added in 2024 to JavaScript): [demoCompleter()] “exits” [complete]/[completeError] from the constructor right from the start, without any additional tricks.
    • To cancel an asynchronous operation (there is no generic [AbortController] in Dart), [cancellableTask] starts the task and uses a [Completer] as a cancellation signal, via [Future.any()] —which works perfectly HERE, since we specifically want the first of the two events, whichever it may be.

    3.9.9. Conclusion

    [Future] and [Completer] together cover everything that [Promise] and its [executor] cover in TypeScript, using a two-step construction rather than a single constructor. The most notable differences concern the recent additions to the [Promise] class: some have never been necessary in Dart ([Completer] has always covered [withResolvers]), while others have no equivalent and must be written by hand ([allSettled], the “real” [any]).

// This TypeScript script is deliberately a COPY of func-04.ts (already
// ported in functions/func_04.dart): it serves as a transition between the
// "Functions" chapter and the "Classes" chapter, by showing that
// JavaScript SIMULATES a class with a simple function (keyword [new] +
// [this] in the body of the function).

// [fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Dart never needed
// this simulation: a Dart function can NOT play the role of a
// constructor (see func_04.dart), so there is simply nothing to
// "simulate" - we directly write a REAL class, which is what the rest
// of this chapter does (class_01.dart and following). This script therefore only
// shows, side by side, the simplest possible Dart class.
class AVerySimpleClass {
  String prop2 = "val2";

  void show() {
    print(prop2);
  }
}

  // instantiation - an automatically generated Dart constructor (here, without
  // parameters) is enough; no special keyword to "make a function
  // play the role of a class" as in JavaScript
  final instance = AVerySimpleClass();
  instance.show();

  // for the "assigning properties/methods afterwards" variant (the
  // 1st example of class-00.ts, with the function [f]), see directly
  // functions/func_04.dart, which details it with "callable classes".
}

    // class_01.dart
// Ports class-01.ts: a class with constructor, getters/setters, and
// toString().
//
// [fundamental difference with TypeScript] the original script simulates
// encapsulation through a naming CONVENTION: a field [_lastName] (with an
// underscore), accessed via a getter/setter [lastName] - but nothing prevents,
// in TypeScript, writing person._lastName = "xyz" from outside the
// class (see the comment in obj_03.dart). In Dart, the [_] prefix IS
// NOT a convention: it is a RULE OF THE LANGUAGE that makes the field
// truly private, inaccessible outside the FILE (the library) where
// it is declared. Here, the class and its use are in the same
// file, so _lastName stays visible in this file - but it would no longer be
// from another file that would import this class (see
// person.dart/teacher.dart, separated into distinct files
// precisely to illustrate this point).
class Person {
  String? _lastName;
  String? _firstName;
  int? _age;

  // constructor - the "this.xxx" syntax as a named/positional parameter
  // is only a Dart shortcut to directly assign a field; here we
  // rather go through the setters, to stay faithful to the original script
  Person(String lastName, String firstName, int age) {
    this.lastName = lastName;
    this.firstName = firstName;
    this.age = age;
  }

  // getters and setters
  String get lastName => _lastName!;
  set lastName(String value) => _lastName = value;

  String get firstName => _firstName!;
  set firstName(String value) => _firstName = value;

  int get age => _age!;
  set age(int value) => _age = value;

  // toString - the Dart equivalent of "JSON.stringify(this)" requires an
  // explicit export of the fields (see obj_02.dart): there is no
  // automatic introspection of the fields of a Dart class, unlike
  // a JavaScript object
  @override
  String toString() => '{"lastName":"$lastName","firstName":"$firstName","age":$age}';
}

// using the class
void main() {
  final person = Person("Poirot", "Hercule", 66);
  // [difference with TypeScript] "person instanceof Person" becomes
  // "person is Person" in Dart (see arr_01.dart for identical(), already
  // encountered, not to be confused with [is] which tests the TYPE, not
  // the identity)
  // [expected] dart analyze reports "unnecessary_type_check" here (the
  // static type of [person] is already [Person]): this is deliberate, to
  // show the syntax of [is] - a warning, not an error.
  print("person=${person.toString()} ${person.runtimeType} "
      "${person is Person}");
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • line 18: [String? _lastName;]: the prefix [_] IS NOT a convention in Dart; it is a LANGUAGE RULE that actually makes the field private, inaccessible outside the FILE (the library) where it is declared—unlike the [_lastName] from TypeScript, which is a mere convention with no actual effect (see obj_03.dart).
    • [person is Person]: the Dart equivalent of [person instanceof Person]—not to be confused with [identical()], which tests IDENTITY, not TYPE.
    • [toString()] must be written explicitly: unlike [JSON.stringify(this)], there is no automatic introspection of a Dart class’s fields.

    The result of the execution is as follows:

    person={"lastName":"Poirot","firstName":"Hercule","age":66} Person true

    // person.dart
// Ports classes/Person.ts: the same class as class_01.dart, but
// extracted into its own file to be reused through inheritance
// (teacher.dart) - exactly as classes/Person.ts is
// reused by classes/Teacher.ts.
//
// [fundamental difference with TypeScript] from HERE on, the [_lastName] field
// (as well as _firstName and _age) becomes TRULY inaccessible from any
// other .dart file that would import this class - including from
// teacher.dart, which nevertheless inherits from it (see the remark on this
// in teacher.dart). This is the concrete, and no longer merely
// theoretical, difference with TypeScript's _name convention.
class Person {
  String? _lastName;
  String? _firstName;
  int? _age;

  Person(String lastName, String firstName, int age) {
    this.lastName = lastName;
    this.firstName = firstName;
    this.age = age;
  }

  String get lastName => _lastName!;
  set lastName(String value) => _lastName = value;

  String get firstName => _firstName!;
  set firstName(String value) => _firstName = value;

  int get age => _age!;
  set age(int value) => _age = value;

  @override
  String toString() => '{"lastName":"$lastName","firstName":"$firstName","age":$age}';
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • Starting HERE, [_lastName]/[_firstName]/[_age] become inaccessible from any other file [.dart] that imports this class —including from [teacher.dart], which nevertheless inherits from it (see teacher.dart below).
    • This is the CONCRETE difference—which is no longer merely theoretical—from the [_lastName] convention of TypeScript: [person.dart] and [class_01.dart] define the SAME class, but only the version isolated in its own file actually reveals this barrier.

    // teacher.dart
// Ports classes/Teacher.ts: simple inheritance with [extends].
import 'person.dart';

class Teacher extends Person {
  String? _subject;

  // constructor - super(...) calls the constructor of the parent class,
  // exactly as in TypeScript
  Teacher(String lastName, String firstName, int age, String subject)
      : super(lastName, firstName, age) {
    this.subject = subject;
  }

  // getters and setters
  String get subject => _subject!;
  set subject(String value) => _subject = value;

  // [remark, a direct consequence of Dart's true privacy] even as a
  // subclass, Teacher can NOT directly access the
  // _lastName/_firstName/_age fields of Person (they are private to the file
  // person.dart, not only to the Person class): Teacher must
  // go through the inherited PUBLIC getters (lastName, firstName, age), exactly
  // like any other code outside person.dart. This is more
  // strict than TypeScript, where a child class can freely read/write
  // this._lastName inherited from its parent class (the _name convention being
  // only a matter of naming, never a real barrier).
}

    Let’s comment on this code:

    • Line 5: [class Teacher extends Person] and [: super(lastName, firstName, age)]: simple inheritance and a call to the parent constructor, using exactly the same syntax as in TypeScript.
    • [WARNING, direct consequence of true Dart privacy] Even as a subclass, [Teacher] cannot directly access the fields [_lastName]/[_firstName]/[_age] in [Person]: they are private to the FILE [person.dart], not just to the [Person] class. [Teacher] must go through the PUBLIC inherited getters, just like any other external code—which is stricter than TypeScript, where a child class can freely read from or write to the [this._lastName] inherited from its parent class.

// Ports class-03.ts: redefinition (override) of an inherited method.
// Like the original TypeScript script, we start again from [Person] but we
// define a LOCAL variant of Teacher (not the one in teacher.dart),
// to add a redefinition of toString() to it.
import 'person.dart';

class Teacher extends Person {
  String? _subject;

  Teacher(String lastName, String firstName, int age, String subject)
      : super(lastName, firstName, age) {
    this.subject = subject;
  }

  String get subject => _subject!;
  set subject(String value) => _subject = value;

  // redefinition of toString - [override] is essential here (compilation
  // error without it): it is what explicitly indicates that we are
  // redefining a method of the parent class, rather than creating a
  // new one by mistake (a typo in the name, for example) - a
  // safety net that TypeScript does not offer
  @override
  String toString() => "[Teacher]${super.toString()}";
}

void main() {
  final teacher = Teacher("Poirot", "Hercule", 66, "detective");
  // [expected] dart analyze reports "unnecessary_type_check" here (the
  // static type of [teacher] is already [Teacher]): this is deliberate,
  // to show the syntax of [is] - a warning, not an error.
  print("teacher=${teacher.toString()} ${teacher.runtimeType} "
      "${teacher is Teacher}");
}

    // class_04.dart
// Ports class-04.ts: polymorphism - a function accepting the base type
// [Person] can also receive any subclass, such as
// [Teacher].
import 'teacher.dart';
import 'person.dart';

// function accepting a Person as parameter (or any subclass)
void show(Person person) {
  // in all cases
  print("parameter=${person.toString()} ${person.runtimeType}");
  // instance of Person - [is] is the Dart equivalent of [instanceof];
  // true for a Person AND for any subclass such as Teacher
  // [expected] dart analyze reports "unnecessary_type_check" here (the
  // static type of the parameter [person] is already [Person]): this is
  // deliberate, to show the base case before the more interesting case
  // below ([person is Teacher]) - a warning, not an error.
  if (person is Person) {
    print("person=${person.toString()}");
  }
  // instance of Teacher - only true if [person] is
  // specifically a Teacher (or a subclass of Teacher)
  if (person is Teacher) {
    print("teacher=${person.toString()}");
  }
}

void main() {
  // calling show with a teacher
  show(Teacher("Poirot", "Hercule", 66, "detective"));
  show(Person("Marple", "Miss", 70));
}
